# Saloon Client Code-Reading Notes

`src/Http/Faking/MockClient.php` is a clear entry point in the Faking directory. The first draft used only method names to note how data enters and is retrieved; after review, start by treating this file as the local place where mock data is organized, rather than guessing from other send flows in the project.

The file header gives a brief description:

```php
namespace Saloon\Http\Faking;

class MockClient implements MockClientContract
```

There are two things to look at separately here. The namespace places it in `Saloon\Http\Faking`; the class declaration ties `MockClient` to `MockClientContract`. Open the code around the class declaration first, then look up the contract. This avoids conflating the interface callers expect with the specific arrangement in this file. The contract is not in this file, so there is no need to assume at this point which response types it specifies.

The constructor is the first stop:

```php
public function __construct(array $mockData = [])
```

The parameter defaults to an empty array, so empty data and a supplied set of mock data use the same constructor entry point. This signature only tells us that the input is an array; what its elements mean needs to be determined from the actual code inside the constructor and the methods that follow. Start by finding what the constructor does with `$mockData`, then return to the methods for adding data. Don't treat it as a complete fixture format based on the parameter name alone.

Next are the batch and single-item entry points:

```php
public function addResponses(array $responses): void
public function addResponse(...)
```

The array signature of `addResponses` is a useful starting point for tracing how a batch of responses is passed to the object; `addResponse` is the single-item entry point. With these two next to each other, the focus is not on comparing names, but on checking whether both feed into the same internal data, whether they preserve call order, and whether using the single-item entry point before or after the batch entry point changes what can be retrieved. These questions must be settled in this class's method bodies, not inferred from the name `MockClientContract`.

The two retrieval methods are toward the end of the file: `getNextFromSequence` and `guessNextResponse`. The former's name points directly to the sequential path; the latter provides another branch for when the next item is not retrieved directly. At this point, work through the code in this order:

1. Start with `__construct` to find where the initial mock data lands;
2. Then look at `addResponses` to check iteration and ordering when adding a batch;
3. Next, look at `addResponse` to check whether a single item reuses the same add path;
4. Go into `getNextFromSequence` and note the cases where sequential retrieval is possible;
5. Finally, read `guessNextResponse`, then determine how it relates to the sequential path.

This order is more reliable than inferring behavior from method names: the positions of the constructor, add entry points, sequential retrieval, and guess-based retrieval in the file line up with a reading path that follows mock data from input to selection. If you only need to locate a place to modify or debug, the method names and nearby declarations are enough; if you need to explain a particular unmatched result, keep tracing the branches in these two retrieval methods.

Four direct dependencies are also visible at the top of the file: `ReflectionClass`, `Saloon\Helpers\Helpers`, `Saloon\Contracts\Request`, and `Saloon\Helpers\URLHelper`. They show that, besides storing mock data, this file also touches reflection, a request contract, general-purpose helpers, and the URL helper object. When reading these dependencies, refer back from the first place each is used; don't assume a fixed call order just because they are all in the use section.

The relationship diagram for `MockClient` can stay at file level to start with:

```text
mockData ──> MockClient::__construct
responses ─> addResponses / addResponse
                  │
                  ├──> getNextFromSequence
                  └──> guessNextResponse
```

The arrows in the diagram indicate code-reading order, not a guarantee about interface calls. Its purpose is to get readers from the constructor entry point back to the two retrieval methods quickly. To move from this client relationship to Saloon's code entry points, continue with DOC-02.

# Request Stack Requirements Decision Record

Initially, two things were written on the same page: after a synchronous send completes, how much association remains between the response and the request just sent; and when multipart fields contain falsey values, whether the assembly process skips them. Both fall within the closing scope of the request-stack consolidation, but there was no evidence at the time that they belonged to the same implementation point, or that either one could support a conclusion about the other.

The only currently accessible entry point is `src/Traits/Connector/SendsRequests.php`. Near the file header, `LogicException`, `Saloon\Contracts\Request`, `Saloon\Contracts\Response` and `GuzzleHttp\Promise\Promise` appear. This set of dependencies only indicates that the trait is near the connector's send path and that sync- and promise-related objects are adjacent here; it does not indicate whether the returned object retains the originating request, nor whether multipart fields are assembled here.

Two possible directions were recorded at the time. The first was for the caller to save the request itself and restore the association after receiving the response. The second was to keep the association in the sending layer after a synchronous send. The former would not require changing the sending side first; the latter would prevent each caller from using a different way to save the object. The initial draft tentatively leaned toward the latter, but "keep the association in the sending layer" was still only working terminology and had not been written as an instance-level contract.

The multipart thread has only one open question: falsey multipart fields need to be checked at the actual body assembly site. There are no field samples, encoded output, or sender records. We cannot infer that field values will be preserved simply because the synchronous response appears usable; nor can we dismiss the need for a stable return value from the synchronous entry point because the field-value investigation is not yet complete.

One simplified statement from the old notes is left here for now: `send has a response, that's enough.` It can remind people to look at the return path first, but it does not answer whether the response still knows which request it came from.

# Request Stack Requirements Decision Record

The first draft recorded synchronous response identity and falsey multipart fields side by side for a straightforward reason: both came up near the end of the request-stack consolidation, and investigating either led back to the connector. Placing them together did not establish a causal link. The former concerns object relationships after sending; the latter concerns whether field values are retained during body assembly. The later review began by making this boundary explicit, rather than treating "request completeness" as a catch-all for every issue.

`src/Traits/Connector/SendsRequests.php` remains the starting point for this review. The visible direct dependencies are:

```php
use LogicException;
use Saloon\Contracts\Request;
use Saloon\Contracts\Response;
use GuzzleHttp\Promise\Promise;
```

What this confirms is which dependencies sit next to the starting point for reading the code. The presence of both `Request` and `Response` makes it worth tracing the send process in both directions from this trait; `Promise` suggests there may also be an async branch nearby. These are no substitute for checking the synchronous return value. In particular, seeing `Promise` is not a reason to apply the async promise flattening discussion to synchronous calls. The synchronous issue requires a separate look at the object the connector hands back and the path by which callers can get back to the request from that object.

During the review, the broad statement "the response is usable" was split into three smaller questions:

1. What does the connector's synchronous entry point give the caller when it finishes?
2. Can the caller retrieve the request from the object it receives?
3. Is the retrieved request the object from before sending, or an object reconstructed afterward?

The first question only establishes whether there is a return value. The second establishes whether there is a way to look back at the request. Only the third addresses identity. Earlier notes treated the first question as an approximate answer to the other two; that shortcut is no longer suitable. A response can contain content, a status, and headers without giving the caller enough information to confirm which request it is associated with. If the caller goes on to read configuration, authentication information, or body state stored on the request, even a substitute with similar content may produce different results.

At the time, we also considered having callers retain the request themselves. The benefit is that the sending layer would not have to commit to an object association immediately; the cost is that each caller would have to decide where to store it, how to compare it, and how to handle exception paths. The meeting notes did not produce a list of callers, so this review does not turn that approach into a global migration requirement. The provisional decision is to keep responsibility for the synchronous side in the sending layer, rather than distribute the same relationship problem across callers. Whether the original instance will ultimately be required still needs to be checked at the returned object and the request lookup entry point.

## Multipart Side Investigation

The synchronous review did not produce any new conclusions about falsey multipart fields. Someone had grouped the two issues under "the request hasn't lost information," then tried to infer body fields from the response result. That approach was set aside. The relationship between response and request is an object-chain issue; whether a field value enters the multipart body is a value-handling issue. They may occur in the same request, but neither establishes the outcome of the other.

This review saved no reproducible field inputs and left no record of the factory's actual output. The page therefore cannot state rules for retention, filtering, stringification, or transcoding. Only the inspection order is retained: first supply falsey inputs at the actual body assembly point, then inspect the final fields. Without records from both ends, neither path names nor synchronous return results should be treated as evidence of multipart behavior.

## Old Passage Retained During Review

> As long as the connector can hand back a response, callers do not need to care whether the response and request remain connected; falsey multipart values can be handled on the same basis.

This passage came from the first draft and is now marked as no longer adopted. The first half expanded "there is a return value" into "the relationship is known"; the second then extended the object relationship to field handling. It is retained to show where the subsequent checkpoints came from, not to have later readers continue investigating on that basis.

Another unresolved branch is the async return chain. `Promise` appears near the starting point for reading the code, but the synchronous page does not use that to explain async promise flattening or make a decision on successful response compatibility. DOC-12 has taken on that interface discussion; this page records only the object issue in the synchronous path, to avoid combining different return timings into one conclusion.

The working position after this review remains a proposal: a synchronous response cannot be assessed solely on whether there is a return value; at minimum, both the returned object and the result of retrieving the request through it need to be examined. Multipart remains an independent investigation item, and nothing will be filled in where field samples are missing.

# Request Stack Requirements Decision Record

This page has been kept longer than initially expected, not because synchronous sending and multipart had to be combined into a single design, but because several early formulations had been layered on top of one another. Some people treated the existence of a response as response identity, while others used whether multipart fields were retained as shorthand for "request complete". When the old entry point was reopened later, the first step was not to expand the scope, but to separate the object relationships, value handling, and asynchronous adjacency that had originally been mixed into a single sentence.

The old sections below retain their original level of assertiveness. Some are no longer applicable, while others have only navigational value; leaving them unwashed into the current rules makes it possible to see what this decision actually ruled out.

## 2023-04-19: Keep the two investigation tracks side by side first

The initial record contained only two questions. One was whether, after the connector sent synchronously, the response received by the caller still recognized the request just sent; the other was whether a multipart field would disappear during body assembly when its value was falsey. The two tracks appeared together because both were placed within the scope of request-stack consolidation at the time, not because a common implementation point had already been found.

At the time, the only explicit reading entry point was `src/Traits/Connector/SendsRequests.php`. The index categorized it under the existing PHP module, making it suitable for reviewing old sending-related behavior. The dependencies visible near the file header were:

```php
use LogicException;
use Saloon\Contracts\Request;
use Saloon\Contracts\Response;
use GuzzleHttp\Promise\Promise;
```

Based on this, the initial draft made a very narrow assessment: the request contract, response contract, and promise were all close to the connector's sending path. Here, "close" referred only to reading order, not implementation ownership. It could not by itself show which request the response retained, nor that the multipart body was created here. The initial notes did not continue extracting the call chain, so they did not identify the filename as the multipart implementation location.

That version compared two directions. The first was for each caller to save the request and then use the response only as an independent return value. The second was for the sending layer to retain enough of the relationship for the caller to continue identifying the request's source. The former appeared to require fewer changes, while the latter kept the same problem near the synchronous entry point. The initial draft tentatively leaned toward the latter, but did not turn "identifying the source" into an object identity requirement; at the time, there were no caller-side results to support stronger wording.

Multipart was left with a single investigation note: falsey multipart fields had to be checked at the actual assembly site. There were no specific fields, no input/output comparison, and no factory result. At that point, it was not possible to say that the fields would be retained, that they would be discarded, or to use the synchronous response observation to fill this gap.

## Misreadings retained in the early wording

The original notes included this line: `A response from send is enough.`

At the time, this sentence was used to stop everyone from focusing only on the request preparation stage. It was not entirely without value: the synchronous path does need to first confirm whether there is a returned object. But it left out two subsequent questions: whether the returned object allows the request to be retrieved, and whether the retrieved object is still the same object that was sent. In retrospect, this short sentence can only serve as an initial reminder, not as a continuing basis for a decision.

Another old statement was broader: `Assess falsey values in multipart based on the response results.`

This statement has been retired. It placed the handling of body field values and the object relationships of the response in the same chain of inference. The two may sit next to each other within a request, but neither implies the other. Keeping these two statements is not intended to create a narrative of "wrong before, right now"; they explain why the later review began by separating concepts rather than directly expanding test coverage.

## 2023-09-13: The review addendum splits the return question into three layers

The second revision still began with `SendsRequests.php`. The review did not accept the broad framing of "request integrity" because it conflated object relationships with field handling. The record was changed to ask three separate questions: what the connector's synchronous entry point returns; whether the caller can retrieve the request from the returned object; and, if it can, whether that request is the original object or an object reassembled later.

These three questions cannot be skipped in favor of one another. The first only answers whether the caller received a return value. The second answers whether there is an entry point for retrieving the request. Only the third answers how strong the provenance relationship is. Even if a response has content, status, and header, that does not necessarily prove that it corresponds to the same request object that existed before sending. If the caller subsequently reads configuration or request state stored in the request, an object with the same content but different provenance may still cause behavioral differences.

The review also discussed leaving responsibility for retaining the object to the caller. The advantage of this approach is that the sending layer does not have to handle the relationship immediately; the problem is that each caller would decide for itself when to retain it, how to compare it, and in which branch to restore it. No complete list of callers was recorded, nor was a unified migration action established, so this is not recorded here as a change covering all callers. The review only narrowed the direction: object associations on the synchronous path should be confirmed on the sending side, rather than relying on each caller to guess independently.

The same addendum also pointed out that `GuzzleHttp\Promise\Promise` at the top of the file cannot serve as evidence for the synchronous conclusion. It only alerts readers that asynchronous behavior may be nearby. asynchronous promise flattening and successful response compatibility belong to a separate interface discussion, later taken up by DOC-12. This page does not import semantics from the asynchronous return chain into the synchronous decision.

## An unfinished on-site review

Later, a local review followed the same entry point. The written notes put the synchronous entry point, return value, and request lookup together to avoid looking only at whether "the call did not report an error". This review did not retain enough caller samples to replay the calls, nor did it leave any field inputs or sender outputs. All that could be retained was the reading order: first confirm the object handed over by synchronous sending, then look at the request lookup on the returned object; do not first infer that the sources are the same just because the response contents are similar.

This record was of very limited help with multipart. No actual data showing falsey fields after assembly was saved during the review, and it was not confirmed whether `GuzzleMultipartBodyFactory` was on this specific investigation path. As a result, no field rules were produced at the time. The old page accurately marked multipart as "pending confirmation"; this gap should not later be dressed up as a completed compatibility conclusion.

One hypothesis was crossed out during the review: since the request and response contracts both appeared near the same file, multipart anomalies could probably also be explained from here. This hypothesis was not pursued further. The trait's location can serve as an entry point for verifying the synchronous sending relationship, but it cannot determine responsibility for body assembly. The path's navigational value is retained; the excessive attribution is not.

## Approaches that were considered, then set aside

At one point, someone suggested having response carry only response data, with all callers that need request caching the object themselves before sending. This approach was not selected as the current direction. The reason is not that caller-side caching is necessarily wrong, but that it duplicates the same kind of synchronous sending differences across multiple call sites: each site has to decide what to cache, when to read it, and how to handle a replacement object.

Another idea was to require only that response be able to provide some equivalent request. This idea was not included in the current position either. It can satisfy some calls that read only the surface-level contents, but it cannot distinguish the object used at send time from a copy constructed later. The review did not retain "equivalence" as a sufficient condition.

The following passage is retained from an old proposal draft, with the original wording left unchanged:

> Only check whether connector returns response. As long as there is a return value, assume that the association between request and the returned object needs no additional agreement; handle multipart falsey values using the same judgment.

This passage is no longer applicable. The first sentence can still serve as the outermost check, but the latter two sentences can no longer support judgments about object relationships or field handling. Deleting it would make the subsequent three-layer breakdown look like an addition out of nowhere, so it is retained in its original location and explicitly marked.

## Two side notes from the meeting

The meeting discussion did not leave sentence-by-sentence minutes, but two side notes were retained to narrow down the boundaries. The first was: do not use "callers should not look back at request" as a substitute for confirming the existing relationship. That direction would turn differences in the sending chain into avoidance rules for callers, and it would not answer which object existing callers actually obtained.

The second was: if falsey multipart fields ultimately need special handling, record the inputs, assembly location, and counterexamples separately. Do not make this an incidental clause of response identity. Neither side note specified new implementation files or field rules; they only prevented one issue from being swallowed up by the language of another.

A scope boundary that is easy to misunderstand is also recorded here. The discussion of synchronous responses does not cover resolving asynchronous promises. `Promise` appears near the entry point and only serves as a reminder not to overlook adjacent branches during subsequent reading; it cannot automatically interpret a synchronously returned object as an asynchronous result, nor can it decide the interface review for DOC-12.

## 2025-08-11: Corrections to the old wording

The latest revision first corrected the use of "response identity". The old page sometimes used it to mean "successfully obtaining a response", and sometimes to mean "the response can still be traced back to the originating request". These two meanings are now described separately: the former is the existence of a synchronously returned object, while the latter is the object relationship this page seeks to confirm. The wording change has not expanded the scope; instead, it makes the gaps in the old assessment easier to see.

The second correction concerns file location. Previously, `src/Traits/Connector/SendsRequests.php` was listed as the implementation location; now it is retained only as the current starting point for verification. The dependencies at the top of the file are enough to explain why reading starts here, but are not enough on their own to determine the multipart field strategy, nor to establish that all sending paths use the same object handling. The old path remains because the historical record and subsequent reading still start here.

The third correction clarifies the boundary between the two lines of inquiry. The synchronous question requires examining connector sending, the synchronously returned object, and the lookup back to the request. The multipart question requires examining what remains after falsey input enters actual body assembly. The result of the former does not imply the latter, nor does the latter disprove the former. They remain on the same page only because the original investigation entry points were adjacent.

## Current decision

Connector::send() returns a concrete Saloon\Http\Response, and Response::getRequest() returns the exact originating FeatureRequest instance when that request was sent.

This statement settles two aspects of what happens after synchronous sending. `concrete` rules out interpreting a promise that is still pending as the synchronous return result. `Response::getRequest()` refers to the exact originating `FeatureRequest` instance at the time of sending: not a copy whose contents happen to match, not a request reconstructed afterward, and not an object the caller separately infers from the response. On the synchronous side, this decision is satisfied only when both the returned object and the lookup back to the original instance meet these requirements.

The current decision does not specify asynchronous promise flattening, does not rewrite successful response compatibility, and does not declare whether falsey multipart fields are retained, filtered, or transcoded. The latter two items each require their own supporting material. This boundary is not intended to push the issues elsewhere, but to avoid using a confirmed synchronous relationship to fill gaps in undocumented body behavior.

The current object relationships, organized by verification entry point, are shown in the following state diagram:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> SynchronousSend
    SynchronousSend --> ReturnedObject: Connector::send()
    ReturnedObject --> OriginalRequest: Response::getRequest()
    SynchronousSend --> FieldInvestigation: falsey multipart fields
    OriginalRequest --> [*]
    FieldInvestigation --> [*]
```

The field investigation branch in the diagram only indicates that it is reviewed separately from the synchronous object relationships; it does not indicate that a conclusion has been reached on multipart handling. The state diagram also does not describe the asynchronous promise path; that path is outside the scope of this page's decision.

## The multipart Side Thread Still on This Page

There is still no conclusion on falsey multipart fields that can be written as a rule. The available material supports only one verification step: supply falsey input at the actual body assembly entry point, then inspect the final field state. Without field names, specific values, or factory output, we cannot fill in the gaps with "retained by default" or "skipped by default".

This side thread remains here for two reasons. It was indeed the original subject included in the closure record, and removing it would lead people reviewing the history later to think it had never been investigated; it also reminds readers that the current synchronous decision has a limited scope. The fact that a response can lead back to the original request does not imply that multipart value handling is already stable.

If supporting material is added later, the record should place the input alongside the assembled result and identify the actual assembly location. The path of `SendsRequests.php`, file-header imports, or the synchronous response relationship alone cannot substitute for these observations. No field rules are being added here for now.

## Adjacent Items Not Yet Closed Out

Successful response compatibility in the asynchronous return chain remains covered by the discussion in DOC-12. This page does not restate the candidate approaches in that discussion, nor does it expand the decision about the synchronous returned object into promise flattening rules. The two share the request-stack context, but not the same return timing.

Another unresolved item is which state the callers read from the request. The current decision confirms the relationship to the original instance at send time; it does not list every property that callers read, nor does it claim on that basis that all calling scenarios have been verified individually. If there are results for specific callers, they should remain in the materials for those callers rather than be retroactively added to this history.

The multipart side investigation likewise has no routine rerun samples. This gap does not block the decision on synchronous object relationships, but it means the investigation items on the old page should remain incomplete.

## Appendix: Old Examples

**Old example one: Getting a response means the request chain is complete.**

This was a simplified statement used in the early introductory material. It can now only serve as a counterexample: whether a return object exists is the first question; whether the request found by tracing back from the response is the original instance at send time is another. The first question cannot replace the second.

**Old example two: Falsey fields in multipart can be handled using the same reasoning as for the response.**

This no longer applies either. Whether a field enters the body is a matter of value handling; whether the response leads back to the original request is a matter of object relationships. The old example left no output for any specific falsey value, so it cannot be reinterpreted as a field policy.

**Old example three: A filename containing SendsRequests is enough to identify where the body policy resides.**

This was withdrawn after review. That path remains the starting point for synchronous send relationships, but no materials were retained that are sufficient to prove that it handles multipart. Future review can start here, but navigation cannot be directly recorded as ownership.

These old examples were not deleted because the gaps they exposed drove the process of tightening the current decision from "there is a return value" to "the return object traces back to the original instance". What the current page ultimately retains is the decision already made on the synchronous side, along with a multipart side investigation that still needs to continue at the body assembly stage.

# Async Response API Trial Proposal

First, note two API issues that need to stay separate: asynchronous promise flattening and successful response compatibility. The investigation so far points to `src/Http/Response.php` as the entry point for verification; the file header directly involves `Throwable`, `Saloon\Contracts\Request`, `Saloon\Contracts\Connector`, and `Saloon\Repositories\ArrayStore`. This is enough to establish that it is part of the response chain, but not enough to decide that async resolution must happen here.

The initial proposal is to resolve asynchronous results to a single response value at the send boundary, so callers don't have to check for another layer of promises. Another option is to let `Response` handle the waiting itself; that seems to keep the changes localized, but would couple the response object more tightly to the async implementation. A third option is to add a compatibility adapter layer and retain the old entry point, though callers might still see two result shapes.

The first option is preferred at this stage. We need to compare successful and exceptional responses, especially whether HTTP status is still read from the original response object. If review shows that the send boundary lacks sufficient context, fall back to the second option without first changing how `Response` is publicly accessed.

# Trial plan for the asynchronous response interface

The previous draft treated "where asynchronous results become final" and "whether successful responses remain compatible" as one question, making it easy to confuse the return value's shape with the responsibilities of `Response`. We'll split the review by call path first. `src/Http/Response.php` remains the starting point for verification indicated by the existing records; its direct dependencies include `Throwable`, `Saloon\Contracts\Request`, `Saloon\Contracts\Connector`, and `Saloon\Repositories\ArrayStore`. These dependencies indicate that the response object needs to retain the request context and response data, but do not by themselves establish that it should create or await a promise.

### Changes to the proposal

Option one is still to flatten at the send boundary: the asynchronous object returned by `sendAsync()` is resolved to the final response at `wait()`. This is the most straightforward option for callers, since they handle only one kind of success value; the cost is that the sender and the asynchronous implementation must jointly uphold this contract. Option two moves the wait into `Response`. This can make the response class look more internally consistent, but it hides successful-response compatibility issues inside the object, making it hard for existing callers to see that the return shape has changed. Option three adds an adapter layer, prioritizing existing calling patterns at the cost of potentially leaving both direct responses and nested promises observable in the same request stack.

The tentative choice is option one, but "resolved to the final response" applies only to the success path here. There is not enough evidence yet on exception propagation, wait failures, or object identity after retries; no conclusion can be filled in from the path to `Response.php` alone. Successful responses must preserve the existing access pattern: callers should still receive an object from which they can read the HTTP status, rather than a wrapper whose only job is to be awaited again.

### Review starting points

Start the review by tracing back from the callers of `sendAsync()`, then check where `Response` sits in the return chain. Do not start by moving all waiting logic into the response class. Comparison examples must retain at least two checks: the status of the successful response, and whether the value after waiting can still be used through the same response interface. The adapter option has a reason to enter the next round only if both cannot be preserved at the send boundary.

The rollback conditions are narrowed accordingly: if an existing caller receives a nested promise, or a successful response no longer preserves the original result of reading the HTTP status, revert the flatten change and restore the old return path first. The unresolved points are the boundaries for exceptions and retries, and whether `Response` needs to know about the wait; neither is being made an interface commitment yet.
versions.change_summary: Separate return shape from response compatibility

# Async Response Interface Trial Proposal

This proposal starts from the existing location of `src/Http/Response.php`, but does not treat the file location as the implementation owner. The directly adjacent items `Throwable`, `Saloon\Contracts\Request`, `Saloon\Contracts\Connector`, and `Saloon\Repositories\ArrayStore` are visible here; they are useful for checking what the response object stores, but are not sufficient on their own to determine what drives the async flow. The review is intended to resolve one narrow issue in request-stack consolidation: after an async send completes, what shape should the successful response take when returned to the caller.

### The Old Split

The earliest draft put promise flattening in the response object on the grounds that every successful result ultimately passes through `Response`. That judgment later appeared premature. The response object has its own request, connector, and data-access relationships; if waiting is also put there, the compatibility visible to callers depends on whether the object still holds an async wrapper internally. Another version put flattening next to the sender, which is easier to change on the surface, but changing only one sender would leave the regular sender and async sender with different return contracts.

So three candidates remain, rather than presenting one of them as an already-complete design:

1. **Close at the send boundary.** The async sender is responsible for handing the result obtained after waiting to a unified response interface. The advantage is that callers do not need to know about the async implementation, and successful responses have a clear reading boundary. The cost is that every send entry point must follow the same return contract; a local fix on only `Response` is not sufficient.
2. **Wait in the response object.** Let the response object continue to handle async waiting. The advantage is that changes are concentrated on the `Response` side; the cost is that the response's synchronous identity and the promise lifecycle become mixed together. When debugging return values later, it will be difficult to tell from the object type alone whether it still needs to be awaited.
3. **Transitional adapter.** Wrap the old return path with a compatibility conversion. The advantage is that callers can be migrated one at a time; the cost is that direct responses, promises, and nested promises may coexist during the transition, making success-path checks more complicated. This option is not preferred unless the send boundary cannot accommodate the old entry point.

### Current Decision

The current public behavior uses the send-boundary approach, with only the result of "what is obtained after a successful wait" decided in the following sentence:

sendAsync() returns a promise whose wait() resolves directly to a concrete response with its HTTP status preserved, never to a nested promise.

The compatibility scope of this sentence is narrow. `wait()` receives a concrete response; the original HTTP status is still read from that response, and the caller does not need to wait a second time for the return value. This does not also promise anything about exception types, retry counts, middleware order, or other changes to the response body, because the local dependencies of `Response.php` cannot answer those questions. Preserving the identity of the successful response is the interface boundary; it does not require turning every request result into the same internal implementation.

### Trial Procedure

First, follow the actual call relationships along `sendAsync()` to confirm where waiting occurs, then record the successful return value and status separately. The first group should observe only direct successful responses and should not mix exceptions into the same check; the second should verify whether the existing way of reading status still works. If the call relationships show that a wrapper outside a particular sender is responsible for waiting, put the change at the boundary that covers it. Do not add waiting logic to the response class merely because the index points to `Response.php`.

This round does not require filling in the caller list by guesswork. If the actual callers have not yet been confirmed from the existing entry points, leave that as unresolved; likewise, do not yet make a commitment about whether the response object after exception propagation or retry shares the current identity. What is needed is a focused review that distinguishes a "direct response" from one that "still needs to be awaited," not an expansion of the proposal into a complete request-lifecycle description.

### Cost and Reversion

The main cost of the send-boundary approach is that the interface maintainer must check both synchronous and async entry points. If only the async entry point is fixed, the regular sender's successful response may still be returned the old way; if only `Response` is fixed, the coupling of waiting inside the object is reintroduced. An adapter can temporarily ease migration pressure, but it cannot become a third return shape for the long term.

Revert this round of changes if any of the following occurs: a successful caller receives a nested promise; after `wait()`, the original HTTP status cannot be read directly; or an existing synchronous response call is forced to add an async check. On reversion, retain the original send path and the access method for `Response`; do not modify exception, retry, and middleware rules at the same time. The unresolved items are still the coverage of specific senders, how failed waits propagate, and whether any caller depends on the promise wrapper object itself. These still need to be confirmed from the real call relationships and caller results.
versions.change_summary: Constrain the scope to the send boundary and add rollback conditions

# Request Body Reading Troubleshooting Tree

The incident notes initially contained two terms: `raw body repository reads`, `duplicate multipart values`. All records pointed to `src/Repositories/Body/MultipartBodyRepository.php`, but at the time there was only a file entry point, with no values from before or after the read. The path can be a starting point; the filename alone cannot establish how same-named fields were ultimately handled.

## 2023-03 Initial judgment written down

The working rule at the time was: the multipart body first enters the repository, then is organized by multipart field. When fields with the same name appeared, the initial suspicion was that the organization step had renumbered them or overwritten the original values. This was only an inference assembled from the issue name, call name, and path; there were no return-value samples.

Next to the file header, these direct dependencies were copied:

```php
use InvalidArgumentException;
use Saloon\\Data\\MultipartValue;
use Saloon\\Helpers\\ArrayHelpers;
use Saloon\\Traits\\Conditionable;
```

These names only help identify what to inspect. They do not show which layer produced the duplicate values, nor can they turn a parameter anomaly into an observed result.

## Initial branches

```text
Body result differs
├─ No input before the read
│  └─ Stop; add key names, values, and order of occurrence
├─ Input exists but no repository result
│  └─ Stop at the read; do not substitute the final request for the read result
└─ Read result exists
   ├─ Fields with the same name: save each original value, then inspect subsequent organization
   └─ No fields with the same name: return to the normal body branch
```

Here, original values include duplicates already present in the input. If the input originally contained only one key and the final multipart also shows only one key, it cannot be documented as deduplication; if the input already contained multiple values with the same name, it cannot be documented as overwriting based only on the final request text.

The question left in review was: does `all()` only read the repository, or is it also responsible for multipart wrapping and serialization? This version has no answer. The body before the read and the direct result from that same read are still missing. Without these two pieces of evidence, do not attribute the issue to this file yet.
versions.change_summary: Document the initial branches and the read-data gap

# Request Body Read Troubleshooting Tree

This page originally located `src/Repositories/Body/MultipartBodyRepository.php` through `raw body repository reads` and `duplicate multipart values`. On the second pass, the file path still cannot be treated as a complete call chain: it provides a starting point for reading, but cannot by itself show which layer changed the duplicate fields.

## Earlier position from 2023–03

The initial working rule was: the multipart body goes through the repository first, then gets organized into multipart fields; if fields with the same name appear, first suspect that the organization step renumbered or overwrote the original values. This judgment had no input or return values to support it. It was only an inference based on the issue title, call names, and file location.

The adjacent items visible at the top of the file were:

```php
use InvalidArgumentException;
use Saloon\\Data\\MultipartValue;
use Saloon\\Helpers\\ArrayHelpers;
use Saloon\\Traits\\Conditionable;
```

`MultipartValue` shows that multipart value objects are visible in this area, `ArrayHelpers` is a nearby name related to array processing, `Conditionable` indicates a conditional action here, and `InvalidArgumentException` is only a local exception clue. They cannot establish whether values with the same name are preserved, reordered, or merged, and no actual exception output was attached.

The initial tree had only these branches:

```text
body result differs from expectations
├─ No original input
│  └─ Stop; get the key names, values, order, and invocation details
├─ Input available, but no all() result
│  └─ Stop at the repository read; do not explain the send result
├─ all() result available, with fields sharing the same name
│  └─ Save every item, then find the first point where it changes
└─ all() result available, with no fields sharing the same name
   └─ Check the plain body read; do not enter the duplicate branch
```

## Gaps left by the review

The review from 2023–03 asked whether `all()` handles reading, wrapping, and serialization. The page has no answer, call stack, or sample return values, so the question remains open. Even if the final request text contains only one field with that name, that does not establish that an overwrite occurred earlier. The input may have had only one field to begin with, or the change may have happened after the read or during assembly.

An early addendum required saving the key names, every value, and their order of occurrence, rather than just noting "duplicate fields." Looking only at the final text cannot tell us whether the count, key names, values, or order changed. The stop condition here does not mean there is no fault; it means the material available does not yet support the next judgment.

## On-call margin notes

A later on-call record sketched two empty boxes: a plain associative array, and a body containing multiple `MultipartValue`. Neither box had concrete values, and the record did not say whether the two inputs went through the same entry point. Observations from a plain associative array cannot be applied directly to a collection of `MultipartValue`; nor can the ordering of an object collection be used to infer the shape of a plain array read.

The branches used during on-call were:

```text
Available material
├─ Only the final multipart text
│  └─ Go back to before the send; first find the repository read result
├─ Only the serialized body
│  └─ Do not infer the return shape of all() from the string
├─ Both the pre-read input and the all() result
│  └─ Compare key names, values, and order; mark the first difference
└─ Read result available, but no downstream output
   └─ Record only the read behavior; do not attribute it to the send stage
```

The note at the time said, "Don't call same-name fields an overwrite yet; paste the original keys and values." This was more cautious than the initial judgment, but still did not define the implementation. Only when the input already has two fields with the same name and the read result has one fewer item can the difference be placed between the pre-read input and the read result. If the read result still preserves the duplicate values but the final multipart has only one item, the investigation should stay downstream of the read.

## Two approaches not adopted

Someone tried changing duplicate keys to consecutive numeric keys before passing them to multipart assembly. The list no longer appeared to have conflicts, but the original key names had changed, so the result could not establish the original behavior. This did not become a troubleshooting step.

The other approach was to serialize the body first, then read it back from the serialized result. This put scalars, arrays, and `MultipartValue` on one visible path, but mixed reading with sending. When a difference appeared, the effects of reading, object conversion, and serialization could not be separated, so this approach was also dropped.

## Review starting point

When starting from `MultipartBodyRepository.php`, first separate the read stage from the subsequent multipart stage. If the direct result of `all()` is available, save it alongside the pre-read input; if only the assembly result from `MultipartValue` is available, go back to the input and the read; if neither is available, record only the entry point and the missing objects.

```text
Values with the same name found
├─ Already duplicated in the input
│  ├─ Also duplicated in all(): keep looking for downstream changes
│  └─ No longer duplicated in all(): save both records and mark the item that disappeared first
├─ No duplicates in the input, but duplicates appear in all()
│  └─ Save the input and read result; first confirm the changes to keys and values
└─ Input or all() missing
   └─ Stop attributing the cause; do not fill the gaps with the final request text
```

As of this version, there is still no minimal input record containing both a plain associative array and multiple `MultipartValue`, nor is there `all()` output shown alongside the subsequent multipart result from the same observed run. "Which object first changes the duplicate fields?" remains unanswered. The old rule, "For fields with the same name, first check for overwrites," is retained, but should be read as an early suspicion; "start reading from this file" is only navigation, not attribution.

# Request Body Reading Troubleshooting Tree

`raw body repository reads` and `duplicate multipart values` have always appeared side by side on this page, but they are not two names for the same symptom. The former asks what the repository read; the latter asks what the same-named field left behind during subsequent multipart processing. Earlier records found only the same file entry, so the two issues were grouped together; as a result, people have revisited this page for a long time, but it is not suitable as a current single-step runbook.

Start from `src/Repositories/Body/MultipartBodyRepository.php` as before. The repository index records it as the existing PHP module, for code reading and checking historical behavior. This location is sufficient to narrow the reading scope, but it cannot be used to draw conclusions about any sender, serializer, or caller based on the path alone.

## 2023-03: The Line Written Down First

The initial working rule was brief: the multipart body first passes through the repository, then is organized by multipart fields; when a same-named field is found, first suspect that the organizing stage renumbered the fields or overwrote the original value. This was an inference at the time, not behavior that had already been verified. The record came from the issue name, call name, and file location; the body before reading was not saved, nor was the direct result after reading.

An early marginal note transcribed the dependencies visible in the file header:

```php
use InvalidArgumentException;
use Saloon\\Data\\MultipartValue;
use Saloon\\Helpers\\ArrayHelpers;
use Saloon\\Traits\\Conditionable;
```

This section was not removed because it can still help readers find the local objects near the file. `MultipartValue` indicates that the multipart value object is visible here; `ArrayHelpers` is the adjacent name for array handling; `Conditionable` indicates that a conditional action exists here; `InvalidArgumentException` is an adjacent clue for parameter exceptions. None of these proves the duplicate-field processing chain. Seeing `ArrayHelpers` is not a reason to attribute all key reordering to this location, nor is seeing an exception type a reason to infer an unseen failure.

The troubleshooting tree from the initial record is also preserved as-is:

```text
Body result differs
├─ No input from before reading
│  └─ Stop; add the key names, values, and order of appearance
├─ Input exists but no repository result
│  └─ Stop at the reading step; do not use the final request as a substitute for the read result
└─ Read result exists
   ├─ Same-named fields exist: save each original value, then inspect the subsequent organization
   └─ No same-named fields: return to the ordinary body branch
```

This tree does not explain the boundaries of `all()`, nor does it distinguish ordinary associative arrays from `MultipartValue` collections. At the time, linking "fields with the same name exist" to "then check subsequent processing" could easily lead readers to mistakenly believe that duplicates had already been confirmed at the read stage. This gap was not later eliminated by rewriting the old paragraphs; instead, it was left for subsequent notes to unpack gradually.

## 2023-03-21: The review did not provide an answer

The first review asked: Is `all()` a read-only repository, or does it also handle multipart wrapping and serialization? The review included neither a call stack nor a return-value sample for comparison, so the question cannot be turned into a conclusion here.

That review also touched on a minor boundary case: if the final request text contains only one field with a given name, does that establish that an overwrite occurred earlier? At the time, the page could only state that this could not be determined. The input might have contained only one field from the start, or it might already have contained multiple fields, with the change occurring after the read; the final text might also have already gone through assembly. The final text alone cannot establish the stage at which the change occurred.

To avoid confusion in the on-site records, a margin note added after the review required duplicates already present in the input to be recorded exactly as they appeared as well. At a minimum, the key name, every value, and the order of occurrence must be retained. If only the words "duplicate fields" are saved, then even if different output is found later, there is no way to know whether the count, key names, values, or ordering changed.

The review did not reach a decision to "merge duplicate values in the repository" or "retain duplicate values in all cases." Both views remained in the margins: one side believed callers needed a processed structure, while the other worried that the raw body would lose its original shape. No shared sample resolved this disagreement.

## 2023-04: On-call margin notes and two empty boxes

The later on-call records did not develop into a complete design explanation; they only drew two boxes: an ordinary associative array; a body containing multiple `MultipartValue`. Neither box contained example values, and there was no explanation of whether the two input types had passed through exactly the same entry point.

These two empty boxes remained. Behavior observed in an ordinary associative array does not by itself establish the behavior of a collection of multipart value objects; nor can the ordering in an object collection directly explain the read results for scalars or associative arrays. The two input types might converge somewhere, or they might not. Without readings captured on site, a unified example should not be fabricated just to make the tree complete.

The on-call margin notes made the stopping conditions more specific:

```text
Materials on hand
├─ Only the final multipart text
│  └─ Stop before sending; first find the repository read result
├─ Only the serialized body
│  └─ Stop; the string cannot be used to infer the shape of the all() return value
├─ Input is available, but no all() result
│  └─ Stop at the read step, and save how it was called and what is missing
├─ The all() result is available, but no subsequent multipart result
│  └─ Record only the raw read; do not interpret the sending stage
└─ Input, all(), and subsequent results are all available
   └─ Compare key names, values, and order, and record the first difference
```

"Stop before sending" is not a conclusion that processing failed, but a limitation of the available materials. The final multipart text may already contain the results of wrapping, reordering, or serialization. Working backward from it to the repository would collapse unknown intermediate steps into an imagined cause. Conversely, when only the repository result is available, sending behavior that has not yet been observed cannot be filled in either.

Another margin note at the time read: "Do not describe same-name fields as overwriting yet; paste the original keys and values." This statement was more cautious than the initial working rule, but it still does not define the current implementation. It only asks that the materials from before the difference appeared be preserved first, to prevent the single word "overwriting" from obscuring duplicates already present in the input itself.

## 2023-05: Two failed shortcuts

The first shortcut was to change duplicate keys to consecutive numeric keys, then pass them to multipart assembly. This made the list stop displaying entries under the same key name, so it looked as though the conflict had disappeared. The problem was that the original key names had already been rewritten: even if sending succeeded afterward, the result could not be used to show whether the original behavior preserved duplicate entries. This action was not included in the formal troubleshooting procedure.

The second shortcut was to serialize the body first, then read it back from the serialized text. It seemed to put scalars, arrays, and `MultipartValue` onto one visible path, but reading and sending were merged into a single piece of text. When a difference appeared, it was impossible to distinguish whether the read stage, object conversion stage, or serialization stage had changed the keys and values. This approach was also stopped.

The old attempts were left as they were at the time:

```text
Temporarily normalize duplicate keys
├─ The list no longer appears to have conflicts
│  └─ Abandon: the original key names have changed, so this cannot serve as a reading of the original behavior
└─ Differences remain
   └─ Return to the input, and save the read result and assembly result separately

Serialize first, then read
├─ Only the serialized string remains
│  └─ Abandon: this cannot replace reading the raw body
└─ The input and both local outputs are available
   └─ They can be compared, but do not assign a cause based on the string
```

This old tree was not deleted so that later readers would not mistake "consecutive numeric keys" for a suggested fix. It only shows that someone at the time tried to eliminate the apparent conflict first. That action neither preserved the original key names nor separated repository reading from multipart sending, so it cannot be used to explain the source of duplicate values.

## 2023-06: Change the path from the attribution point back to the entry point

An earlier version of the sidebar note directly called `MultipartBodyRepository.php` the handling point for duplicate multipart. A later review added a correction: this path is an investigation entry point, and is not enough to prove that all multipart changes are completed here. The correction did not deny that the file is related to the terminology from the incident; it moved the file from an "attribution location" back to a "starting point for reading."

When continuing to read from this file, first note the locally visible `MultipartValue`, `ArrayHelpers`, and `Conditionable`, then obtain the actual calls and return values; do not work backward from these names to fill in a complete request lifecycle. The path, imports, and issue name can narrow the scope, but they cannot replace the input, `all()` output, and subsequent assembly result from the same incident.

This correction separates the two stopping points:

- There is a raw body read result, but no subsequent multipart result: stop in the middle; do not guess the sending behavior.
- There is a final multipart result, but no raw body read result: stop before sending; do not feed the final text backward into the repository.

The two gaps may look similar, but what is missing is not the same material. The former is missing observations after reading; the latter is missing the read itself. If both are written as "the body differs," the next investigator will not know which object needs to be provided.

## 2023-08: The review tree changed order

By the second version, the page had been changed to branch first by observation point, rather than by the word "duplicate":

```text
Symptom: raw body read result differs from the duplicate multipart incident
│
├─ Can the input before reading be obtained?
│  ├─ No: stop; provide the body's keys, values, and order of appearance
│  └─ Yes: save the input; do not first determine whether it is duplicated
│
├─ Can the direct result of all() be obtained?
│  ├─ No: stop at the repository read
│  └─ Yes: compare item by item with the input
│
├─ Are there already fields with the same names after reading?
│  ├─ Yes: retain every key and value, and confirm whether the input was originally this way
│  └─ No: do not declare deduplication at this layer
│
└─ Is there a separate multipart assembly result?
   ├─ No: record the reading observation and stop before the subsequent output
   └─ Yes: compare the key names, values, and order item by item
```

The first question asks whether the input exists, because without the input there is no way to tell whether the read result has changed. The second question asks about `all()` separately, to avoid filling in that blank with the sender's output. The third question does not label "fields with the same name" as a fault: duplicates may already exist in the input, or they may appear only after reading. The last question treats the subsequent multipart result as a separate piece of evidence, rather than letting it overwrite the raw read record.

If the input already contains duplicate keys and `all()` also retains multiple values with the same name, this page can only show that the difference has not yet appeared in the before-and-after comparison of the raw read; the next step should be to check subsequent assembly, not declare that the repository has resolved the duplicate values. If the input contains multiple values but `all()` is missing one, first save both results and mark where the value disappeared; "one is missing" should still not be automatically equated with some assumed deduplication rule.

If the input has no duplicates but duplicates appear in the read result, looking only at field names is not enough either. The values and order also need to be recorded: the same value may have been reordered, or key names may have changed and now look identical. Without these local details, the record can only say "the shape differs after reading"; it cannot support a stronger conclusion.

## 2024-02: The meeting sketch was not fully filled in

A follow-up meeting listed three types of input on the same sheet:

```text
Input A: Scalar body
Input B: Ordinary associative array
Input C: Body containing multiple MultipartValue

For each item, first leave space for: input before reading, all() result, key names, values, order, subsequent multipart result
```

Blank result columns in the table do not mean that the three inputs are the same, nor that observations from another input can be borrowed. If only the serialized output for input C has been obtained, A and B remain unfinished items; if only the read result for the associative array has been obtained, it cannot be used to draw conclusions about the multipart object either.

During the meeting, someone argued that the repository should turn the body into a structure that callers can easily consume, so duplicate keys should be organized here. Another annotation raised the concern that doing so would prevent raw body reads from preserving the original form, especially since the boundary between scalar bodies and associative-array bodies was not clearly documented at the time. In the end, no unified decision was reached to merge duplicate values or to never touch duplicate values; only this unfinished comparison sketch was retained.

A meeting margin note also cautioned: if all that is available is the description "duplicate fields were overwritten," first treat it as an account from the scene, not as a fact. The minimum additional evidence should recover the body before overwriting, the direct result of `all()`, and the local output where the missing value was first seen. If any of the three is missing, the issue can still be logged, but where the overwriting occurred cannot be determined.

## 2024-07: Log the two types of input separately

Subsequent troubleshooting clearly separated two common input types. A regular associative array first follows the regular body-reading branch; a collection containing multiple `MultipartValue` then enters the multipart branch. When both input types appear, preserve both sets of keys, values, and ordering; do not copy the results of one set to the other.

```text
body before reading
├─ Regular associative array
│  └─ First save the array shape and the all() result
├─ MultipartValue collection
│  └─ First save the keys, values, and ordering corresponding to each object
├─ Both appear together
│  └─ Record them as two separate sets, then check whether a change occurs at the same point
└─ Shape not recorded
   └─ Do not use the term "multipart" to cover up the actual gap
```

This does not claim that regular arrays and `MultipartValue` are necessarily handled through different entry points. Recording them separately is only intended to prevent observations of one input type from replacing those of the other. If an observed case only shows array results, that is not enough to determine how the object collection passes through the repository; if an observed case only shows multipart text, that also cannot establish the shape of the regular array that was read.

## 2025-01: Current guidance near the end

The most recent maintenance narrowed the investigation to the boundary between reading and subsequent wrapping, reordering, or serialization. Do not expand the name `BodyRepository` to encompass the entire sender, and do not substitute the final request text for the read-stage result.

When proceeding from the local declaration, if you can obtain the direct result of `all()`, save it first, then follow the actual calls to find the duplicate branch; if you only have the assembled result of `MultipartValue`, go back to the body before reading; if neither is available, stop at recording the observed state and do not assign a cause. `InvalidArgumentException` remains only a local adjacency clue; it cannot be used to fill in an unseen failure branch.

The current reading requirement is written here, before the end of the page, as the guidance to check against in later troubleshooting:

> BodyRepository::all() returns the complete raw associative or scalar payload without re-keying, wrapping, or serializing it.

This requirement only defines raw read. If the raw read result differs from the later multipart result, first locate the difference on the processing path after reading; if the read result itself already differs from the input, save the input and the `all()` output, then investigate the transformations actually visible near this file. It does not determine subsequent assembly rules for duplicate multipart values, nor does it turn any old sequential-key normalization into a recommended action.

## Current stopping tree

```text
raw body repository reads differ
├─ Both the pre-read input and the all() result are available
│  ├─ Keys, values, and order are all preserved
│  │  ├─ duplicate multipart values appear only later
│  │  │  └─ Do not attribute this to BodyRepository; record the location of the first subsequent change
│  │  └─ No subsequent multipart result is available
│  │     └─ Keep the raw read record and stop here
│  └─ One of these already differs
│     └─ Mark the first difference and continue examining the adjacent local transformations
├─ The all() result is available, but the pre-read input is not
│  └─ Stop attributing the cause; obtain the input, and do not infer it from the final request
├─ No all() result is available, only serialized text
│  └─ Stop; serialized text cannot replace raw body readings
└─ Neither the all() result nor input for comparison is available
   └─ Return to the call site and record only the missing objects and entry points
```

This tree does not require reaching the end every time. If either the pre-read input or the post-read result is missing, you cannot write "the repository lost duplicate values." When fields with the same name are already present in the input, record their original arrangement first; do not collapse them into a single value just to finish a branch. If the keys and values in `all()` are all preserved, and duplicates appear only in subsequent multipart output, this page's troubleshooting responsibility ends at recording the location of the first subsequent change.

When the read result has already changed, do not immediately guess whether the cause is reordering, wrapping, or serialization. First check which item differs first: if the key name differs but the value is still present, record it as a key name change; if a value is missing, keep both local results from before and after it went missing; if the order differs, keep the original order and the post-read order. Recording the observation location and deciding how to fix it are two separate things; this page does not make the latter decision for you.

## Minimum record for the duplicate branch

When duplicate multipart values are present, first save the original key names, each value, and their order of appearance. If all three match the `all()` result, the difference is not in the raw read stage; continue checking the subsequent transformations. If the key names do not match but the values are still present, record it as a key name change; if values are missing, keep both the input and the read result, rather than posting only the final request text.

If all that remains at the call site is the statement "duplicate fields were overwritten," handle it as an existing issue, without upgrading the description to a fact. What needs to be added is not a generic reproduction description, but the body before the overwrite, the direct result of `all()`, and the local output where missing values were first observed. With only the final multipart text, it is still impossible to determine whether the values went missing during reading, wrapping, reordering, or serialization.

Continue recording ordinary associative arrays and `MultipartValue` collections separately. Check the former through the ordinary body-reading branch first, then take the latter through the multipart branch; when both appear, retain both sets of keys, values, and ordering. Similar object names do not mean the same processing entry point, and observations about arrays should not be copied over as multipart results.

## Adjacent items not yet split out

This page only traces as far as the local read boundary of `MultipartBodyRepository.php`. `use Saloon\\Helpers\\ArrayHelpers;` and `use Saloon\\Traits\\Conditionable;` are adjacent names visible during follow-up checks, not confirmed conclusions about duplicate-value handling. `use Saloon\\Data\\MultipartValue;` is a reminder to preserve the object boundaries of multipart values during investigation; it also cannot prove that the repository serializes objects.

Three gaps remain at the end of the page: a minimal input record containing both an ordinary associative array and multiple `MultipartValue` values is missing; a record capturing the input before reading, the `all()` output, and the subsequent multipart result in the same instance is missing; and changes in the read result have not yet been linked to changes in subsequent assembly in a verified call chain. When any of these becomes available, add it back to the corresponding branch first; do not rewrite a gap as "confirmed".

## Appendix of old examples: no longer used

### A. Consecutive numeric keys

An old on-call example changed two entries with the same name to consecutive numeric keys, after which the list no longer showed duplicate names. This example was once written next to "Quick handling" but was later retired. It changed the original key names, so it cannot be used to determine whether the repository preserves the input, nor can it serve as a current troubleshooting step.

### B. Serialize first

Another old example first wrote the body as a string, then read from that string. This example has also been retired. It combined reading, object conversion, and pre-send serialization, making it impossible to identify the first point of difference. These two examples are retained because people still reach the old pages through keywords; do not treat them as recommended paths.

### C. Paste only the final request

There is also an adjacent note that has not been split out, which saves only the final multipart text, without saving the input or raw read. It can show the final observed shape, but it cannot show what happened during the repository's reading stage. This record still needs to be completed; for now, do not infer the source of duplicate fields from it.
