# Retry Behavior Requirements Decision Record

The old starting point for this page was very narrow: the investigation moved from the issue name and call name to `src/Http/Faking/MockClient.php`. Early records therefore considered the response sequence of `MockClient` together with the retry attempt history, and also treated exponential retry intervals as something that might be explained by the same place. This entry-point-oriented view remains in the archive, but it can no longer be treated as the implementation ownership.

What the file itself can confirm is limited. `MockClient` implements `MockClientContract` in `src/Http/Faking/MockClient.php:19`; `__construct` accepts `array $mockData = []`, while `addResponses` and `addResponse` are located where responses are added, followed by `getNextFromSequence` and `guessNextResponse`. The direct dependencies visible in the file header include `ReflectionClass`, `Saloon\\Helpers\\Helpers`, `Saloon\\Contracts\\Request`, and `Saloon\\Helpers\\URLHelper`. These declarations are sufficient to show how samples enter the mock and how responses are retrieved, but not how waiting is scheduled during request execution.

The first direction considered early on was to treat the fixed response queue as the retry history. `addResponses` can contain failed and successful responses, and the retrieval order is easy to replay. It is useful for answering "Which response was obtained first?", but the order alone cannot answer whether the request actually waited or whether a failure triggered another attempt. This conflation from the old notes is retained as a working hypothesis, but was not expanded further.

The second direction was to trace back from the call results. A successful call and a failed call must be considered separately here: first record the state before the call, then inspect what was actually left after the call ended. If all that is observed is that one element was removed from the mock queue, that is still only the phenomenon of a sample being retrieved; it cannot automatically become request history or replace observation of the path after a failure.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "MockClient Input Sample" as Sample
    state "Response sequence retrieval" as Sequence
    state "Successful/failed call results" as Result
    state "retry attempt history observation" as History
    state "exponential retry intervals to reproduce" as Interval
    [*] --> Sample
    Sample --> Sequence
    Sequence --> Result
    Result --> History
    Sample --> Interval
    Interval --> [*]
```

The decision left after review was not to merge the two observations, but to keep them separate. MockClient continues to serve as the place for preparing repeatable inputs; the retry count, history, and waiting intervals must be determined separately from the results after request execution. This means giving up a seemingly convenient unified field, but it avoids miswriting fixture data retrieval behavior as the sender's timing behavior.

SAL-206 narrow the scope of result-side observation to two types of calls: one successful call and one failed call, each of which must leave a visible result for the retry attempt history. The focus here is "What was left after the call?", not how many items the queue consumed. The successful and failed paths cannot share an unchecked sequence description; if the failed call leaves no additional visible record, only that observation is retained.

SAL-223 leave another item pending: reproduce the "exponential retry intervals" starting from the pre-call state, and then confirm whether any additional visible change appears after completion. The current material provides no interval values, waiting formula, or confirmed successful sample, so this page still describes it as a reproduction task rather than an established rule. This item came later than the early entry-point record and cannot be backported into v1.

## Approaches Not Adopted

Old approach A was to have the mock response order represent the retry attempt history. Its advantage is that a failure-then-success sample is easy to replay; its disadvantage is that it mistakes "the response was retrieved" for "the request was attempted again." It is retained because it still explains why the investigation originally started from MockClient; it no longer determines behavior.

Old approach B was to add exponential retry intervals directly to MockClient. This would make the samples and waiting time appear to be handled in one place, but the test double would then start taking on the scheduler's responsibilities. The fixture, which originally expressed only response matching, would also be forced to carry timing semantics, and changing the queue implementation could change the observed retry results. No material supports this compatibility cost, so the approach was not retained.

Old approach C was to save only the last successful response. It is the simplest option for an ordinary successful call, but it leaves a failed call without comparable history and cannot answer what the successful and failed calls each left behind. This approach can explain the "final result," but it cannot serve as the complete choice for this record.

The review did not create another object to cover every case. The retained boundary is narrower: input samples, response retrieval order, call results, and whether additional history appeared are recorded separately. This leaves the page without a neat unified chain, but it still distinguishes mock facts from the retry aspects that remain to be investigated.

## Changes Left by Follow-up Verification

v2 added a record of an actual verification, but did not erase the unconfirmed parts. When investigating this line now, start with the input and sequence retrieval from `MockClient`, then observe the results of the successful and failed calls separately; only continue checking the waiting intervals when the pre-call state can be reproduced. The verification provided no interval value that can be written into this page, and did not prove that a particular additional history is necessarily retained after a failure.

This keeps the responsibilities of `__construct`, `addResponses`, and `addResponse` on the sample-preparation side. `getNextFromSequence` and `guessNextResponse` can help locate how responses are selected, but cannot be written up as evidence of a backoff strategy. If a verification reproduces only the response order, the record stops there; if no waiting or additional history is observed, an ideal attempt sequence is not filled in.

SAL-206 serve as navigation for observing successful/failed results, and SAL-223 serve as navigation for reproducing intervals. The two cards have different purposes, and one cannot replace the other. `src/Http/Faking/MockClient.php` remains the verification entry point for this page; it has not been rewritten as the overall entry point for the request execution process.

## Verification Boundaries of This Record

This reorganization also leaves one area that is easy to confuse: sample order, call results, and waiting intervals all appear on the page, but the strength of their evidence is not the same. Sample order can be checked directly from the addition and retrieval entry points of MockClient; the results left by a successful or failed call must be recorded by returning to the corresponding call site; waiting intervals are valid only when both a reproducible pre-call state and time observations are complete. The three columns are recorded side by side so that whoever takes over later knows which column already has supporting material and which remains an open question, not to imply that the three columns have already formed an implementation chain.

The review also reconfirmed the relationship between the versions. v1 preserves why the investigation originally started from MockClient, and why history and interval were first separated; v2 adds the verification method, abandoned approaches, and compatibility concerns. v2 did not rewrite v1 as an incorrect conclusion, because the old entry point still explains how SAL-206 and SAL-223 were raised. Reading only the final paragraphs would lose this origin; looking only at v1 would again mistake sampling behavior for retry behavior. Both versions need to be retained together so that the conclusion does not become detached from the conditions under which the judgment was made.

During handoff, record four items separately: which failed and successful samples were prepared, which type of call was actually executed, which results were visible after the call, and whether reproducible waiting was measured. If any item is missing, leave the gap as-is; do not fill it with the queue length, the last response, or the expected formula. This will not answer the unfinished SAL-223, but it will prevent a later verification from misreporting an easily replayed mock sequence as already-verified exponential backoff.

This also explains why this page does not specify a unified retry data structure. The current material supports only retaining the observation boundaries; if a history object, timing hook, or new scheduling entry point is added later, its compatibility cost should be documented in a new decision record and linked back to this page, rather than retroactively writing the new design as a choice that already existed at the time.


## Decision Currently Retained

retry attempt history and exponential retry intervals will continue to be maintained separately. The former first asks what visible results a successful call and a failed call each leave behind; the latter then asks whether the waiting intervals can be reproduced from the pre-call state, and whether any additional history appears after reproduction.

Therefore, the response sequence can serve as input material, but cannot by itself prove the number of retries or the waiting behavior. The old approaches and their compatibility costs remain here because they explain the evolution of the requirement; the conclusion of this page remains limited to the verified scope. If SAL-223 is completed later, what needs to be added is interval observation and compatibility impact, not renaming the mock entry point as the retry implementation.

versions.body:
# Digest Authentication Decision Record

The draft recorded the digest authentication tuple near PendingRequest because the issue name, pending request, and configuration all pointed to `src/Http/PendingRequest.php`. This entry is useful for reading, but the original sentence "digest authentication is in the pending request" conflated two different questions: where the authentication parameters are organized, and whether the parameters have already become part of the request to be sent.

After review, the file's responsibilities were not expanded. PendingRequest remains the request-side lookup entry; it is not thereby designated as the authenticator, nor is it the sole source of the digest authentication format. This record answers only a narrower question: when someone reports that the digest authentication result is not as expected, where should we first confirm what the request carried?

## The Draft's Three Options

The first option was to describe PendingRequest as the digest authentication implementation. It seemed like the easiest approach: readers could enter the file through the issue name and directly connect the request object with authentication behavior. But this wording would misstate "can see the configuration" as "is responsible for producing the configuration." The request object is midway through the lifecycle; the visibility of authentication-related data there does not mean that the username, password, and digest type are decided or assembled there.

The second option was to retain only the path and make no judgment. This would avoid taking over the authenticator's responsibilities, but it would strip the record of its decision-making value. People later reviewing it would still have to guess whether to start from the request object, the configuration helper, or the sending path; different people could easily enter from different locations and conflate saved state with the source of the parameters.

The third option separates the entry point from ownership. The path provides the first reading location, the configuration key provides the inspection target, and the source of the tuple continues to be traced through the actual reference relationships. The draft already leaned in this direction, but it did not clearly state that this was a decision about the investigation boundary, rather than a complete description of ownership within the authentication stack.

This time, the third option was adopted. It preserves the request-side conclusion supported by the existing material and avoids assigning creation responsibility to PendingRequest based only on the filename or issue name.

## Current Decision

When dealing with a digest authentication tuple, first check `auth` at the configuration boundary of PendingRequest. Digest authentication writes the tuple consisting of the username, password, and digest type to the `auth` key in the pending request configuration.

This sentence limits the result visible on the request side. It does not define parameter validation for the authentication object, specify default values, or state whether the tuple is written when the request is created, when the configuration changes, or at a later stage. Keeping these matters separate allows later review to distinguish between "the authentication side did not form the input" and "the request side did not save the result."

The current decision also does not require stopping the investigation at PendingRequest. When the configuration exists, the actual call relationships must still be followed to find the write point; when the configuration does not exist, we cannot immediately conclude that the authenticator has failed. We must also distinguish between the tuple never being generated and the tuple being generated but not saved afterward. This branch is closer to a locatable request state than "digest authentication has failed."

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Request-side verification" as RequestCheck
    state "`auth` key" as AuthKey
    state "Continue tracing the write point" as TraceWriter
    state "Distinguish generation from saving" as Split

    [*] --> RequestCheck
    RequestCheck --> AuthKey: Inspect PendingRequest configuration
    AuthKey --> TraceWriter: Configuration exists
    AuthKey --> Split: Configuration missing
    TraceWriter --> [*]
    Split --> [*]
```

The end states in the diagram do not mean that the issue has been resolved; they mean that the fixed inspection sequence in this record ends there. Subsequent write points, the authentication object, and the sending implementation belong to their respective call relationships. No additional ownership can be inferred from this state diagram.

## Why the Inspection Point Is on the Request Side

The direct dependencies visible at the file header include:

```php
use Saloon\Enums\Method;
use Saloon\Helpers\Config;
use Saloon\Helpers\Helpers;
use Saloon\Contracts\Request;
```

These adjacent objects place PendingRequest at the intersection of request methods, the request contract, and configuration handling. For this record, that is precisely why it was selected as the inspection entry point: if the authentication parameters have already entered the pending request, they should be verifiable on the request-state side.

However, `use Saloon\Helpers\Config;` only indicates that the configuration helper logic is adjacent to the current file. It does not mean that this helper object defines the digest authentication format, nor that all authentication configuration is written here. Likewise, `Request` and `Method` can show that the file is located within the request lifecycle, but they cannot establish that it is responsible for network negotiation or authentication policy. The value of the path in the draft is retained, but these dependencies are no longer treated as evidence of the tuple's source.

This is also why the decision was not placed at the sender. The sending stage may consume the request configuration, but this time we first need to confirm whether the corresponding state has already been retained on the request. If readers start from the sender, they see values that have already been read or transformed by later paths, making it easy to miss cases where the request side never saved the state in the first place when tracing backward to the write location.

## Old Judgment That Was Changed

The draft implicitly contained an overly broad working assumption: once the digest authentication call was found, the result of the tuple had also been found. This assumption is no longer adopted. A call site can explain only one side; it may show where the authentication parameters enter the flow, but it cannot replace confirmation of the request configuration.

The opposite misreading must also be prevented: after entering through `src/Http/PendingRequest.php`, seeing configuration handling and directly modifying or interpreting the digest authentication parameters themselves. That skips the source of the tuple. Even if the request ultimately contains some configuration, this file alone cannot explain why the username, password, and digest type reached the request side in that form.

Therefore, the current decision treats "constructing the tuple" and "saving the tuple" as two observation points. The former requires examining the actual authentication call chain; for the latter, first inspect `auth` in PendingRequest. They may occur in nearby call sequences, but they are not interchangeable conclusions.

## Compatibility Trade-offs

This time, no separate local storage detached from the request state was created for the digest authentication tuple. Using the existing `auth` on the request side as the verification point allows subsequent paths to work with the same pending request configuration. If the digest data were kept only in some temporary object, it would be difficult during investigation to determine which value was actually used before sending, and the authentication-parameter issue would become a state-synchronization issue between objects.

The compatibility trade-off here is not a claim that all authentication types use the same internal process; it is about avoiding the conflation of the responsibilities of the request object and the authentication object. PendingRequest is responsible for providing inspectable request state; creation responsibility remains with the actual authentication call relationships. This way, future changes on the authentication side will not be mistaken, because of this record's wording, for changes to the request object's responsibilities.

We had considered using `Config` as the primary entry point for digest authentication. The reason for rejecting it is not that it is unrelated to the request, but that the existing material confirms only its direct dependencies in the file and does not confirm its specific read/write role for the digest parameters. Substituting the helper object's name for the actual call relationships would be more prone to overinterpretation than using PendingRequest as the inspection entry point.

## Questions Outside This Record

The following questions have not yet resulted in a decision: at exactly which stage the tuple is written; who determines the final value of `auth` when multiple authenticators participate simultaneously; the precedence order when request-level configuration overlaps with higher-level configuration; whether the sending path converts the parameters again after reading this key; and how missing digest types or incomplete input are handled.

These questions should remain subjects for follow-up verification rather than being filled in with guesses. The current material supports the request-side inspection sequence, but not the implementation details of the branches above. If the actual write location is found later, its source and call relationships should be added to the record for the corresponding object; this record should continue to maintain only the entry point, inspection key, and responsibility boundary.

When handling similar reports, start with the configuration state of `src/Http/PendingRequest.php`. After confirming whether `auth` exists, follow the result to the write point or to the generation-versus-saving branch. This avoids mistaking the request object for the authentication implementation and also avoids missing the state actually saved by the pending request merely because the authentication call was confirmed.

# Request Body Repository Trial Proposal

R26.09 When merging the request stack, don't initially treat multipart as an ordinary array on the request-body side. The existing investigation entry point is `src/Repositories/Body/MultipartBodyRepository.php`; it's already close to `MultipartValue`, `ArrayHelpers`, and `Conditionable`, which indicates that this area needs to both retain multipart values and handle conditional appends and array normalization. API compatibility should be contained at this boundary first, so callers don't each have to guess where empty values, duplicate values, and streaming reads belong.

The tentative trial direction is to retain a narrow interface that represents a "request body repository," with multipart as one implementation rather than making the sender recognize every input shape directly. Callers should depend only on repository operations such as retrieving values, setting them, and checking empty state; the specific multipart parts should still be stored by the implementation. This lets later body types share an entry point, but the cost is that existing fluent syntax may need to pass through an adapter layer instead of continuing to be passed according to the current container's internal structure.

What needs to be run first is not the full sending chain, but several partial inputs through the public entry point: an empty repository, a single `MultipartValue`, multiple values with the same name, and the case where nothing is appended because the condition is not met. Each time, record only what is returned or thrown, and preserve the input order. `InvalidArgumentException` already appears in this file's direct dependencies; during the trial, confirm whether it is merely input protection inside the implementation. Do not use it to classify every incompatibility as an argument error.

There are currently two viable approaches:

| Approach | Handling | Main cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repository interface with an adapter | Leave the existing multipart implementation in place, with callers reading or writing through the interface | Need to clarify which legacy methods remain visible |
| Unified conversion before sending | Have the sending side convert the repository into a multipart payload | The sending side will know the body details again |

Try the first approach first. It keeps the compatibility issue at the body boundary and makes it easier to verify whether conditional changes actually changed the repository contents. Keep the second as an option: if the interface layer cannot express same-name values or the read order of the raw body, revisit whether conversion before sending loses less information.

Judge the retraction conditions at the same boundary: if the adapter requires callers to identify internal multipart values, or if an empty repository cannot be distinguished from an unset repository, stop advancing it as a public interface. At that point, retain only the current implementation, record the inputs it cannot express, and redefine the interface. The unresolved question is whether raw body reads should share the same return contract as multipart; start by checking the declarations and actual entry-point results in this file.

```text
│  │  │  └─ method does not yet exist
│  │  │     └─ Record the missing state and stop at request creation
│  │  └─ Have only the entry name, with no object snippet
│  │     └─ The entry is known, but the relationship is unconfirmed; fill in the actual call path
│  └─ Can identify only the directory or issue name
│     ├─ The directory contains a verifiable real path
│     │  └─ Save the path and wait for the corresponding object being entered
│     └─ Have only the issue name
│        └─ Do not infer the call relationship from the file path
├─ B. Did Config or Helpers change the branch?
│  ├─ Have the original value and the helper return value
│  │  ├─ Behavior changes after changing only Config
│  │  │  └─ Record the before-and-after values, then confirm whether the request is still the same one
│  │  ├─ Behavior changes after changing only the helper input
│  │  │  └─ Record the input and return value; do not casually attribute it to Config
│  │  └─ Both change at the same time
│  │     └─ The conditions were not separated; retain this as unconfirmed
│  └─ Do not have the original value
│     └─ Do not clear the configuration to manufacture a seemingly clean result
└─ C. Does the clue point to connector body merging?
   ├─ Yes
   │  └─ Switch to DOC-24; when returning, add back only the objects that actually appear on the PendingRequest side
   └─ No
      └─ Stay on this tree; do not expand it to the entire sender chain
```

## Entry Points and Old Assessment in the File

Early records placed the anomaly boundary before and after the creation of PendingRequest. The only basis was the direct adjacency visible in `src/Http/PendingRequest.php`:`Method`,`Config`,`Helpers` and `Request`. At the time, these four names were recorded side by side to make it easier to find the entry point by following the order in which the request enters and leaves; this can help locate the file, but cannot determine whether the stray request was brought in from upstream or appeared after local assembly.

> Old assessment: If the stray request appears here, first check the assembly performed by PendingRequest itself.

This sentence remains in the historical section. It provides no evidence about the object before entry, and does not separate the configuration value from the helper return value, so it can now serve only as an early working hypothesis. A rerun that does not show the same behavior is not sufficient to rewrite it as a fix having taken effect.

The file's direct dependencies can still serve as check-back points:`use Saloon\\Enums\\Method;`,`use Saloon\\Helpers\\Config;`,`use Saloon\\Helpers\\Helpers;`,`use Saloon\\Contracts\\Request;`. These declarations indicate that the investigation should begin with the local relationships among method, configuration, helper, and request. They do not themselves provide the caller directory or identify ownership of the anomaly.

## How to Record Branch Findings

When objects before and after entry can be captured, first compare the state changes of the same request. If method already exists but the request does not change before and after assembly, PendingRequest remains a trace-back entry point, but is not the origin point; the snippet should be carried back upstream. Only when a change actually appears after local progression should you continue following the local statements in this file. When method is missing, record only the missing state; do not characterize the caller based on this empty state.

When there is only directory structure, retain the paths that actually appear in the directory and note that no object has been entered yet. When there is only a call name, retain the call name and anomaly location; do not treat the call name as a call edge. The two types of gaps cannot both be written as "call chain pending completion": the former lacks the object, while the latter may not even have a confirmed entry relationship. When the anomaly location cannot be obtained, do not infer it from the path of `PendingRequest.php`.

The original values must be retained for configuration branches. If changing Config makes the behavior disappear, this only shows that the configuration condition changed; if changing the helper input changes the behavior, record the input and return value separately. If both were changed, this cannot establish which condition took effect. A clean result after clearing the configuration does not mean that the original request path has been restored, because it has not been proven that the request is still the same one.

## Marginal Notes Left After Review

One review first confirmed the scope of the issue and then returned it to the actual maintainer; later records still indicated one unconfirmed point in stray request prevention. This change only narrowed the maintenance entry point; it did not narrow the issue to a definite origin location. Therefore, retain the early broad assessment, but place it at the tree's entry point and no longer make it responsible for attribution.

Recovery actions must not be conflated either. Rerunning a scenario without the same call entry only shows that it was not reproduced this time; if the behavior disappears after clearing Config, that only shows that the configuration condition was removed; changing the body from the connector side addresses only the connector body merging clue. None of the three results can replace the request snippets before and after entry. If the issue can be reproduced but there are no snippets, stop at the object gap; if there are snippets but no stable entry point, stop at the call-relationship gap; only when both are available should you compare the differences after changing a single condition.

If the issue is handed off to connector body merging at the scene, DOC-24 are the adjacent check-back pages. When returning here, retain only the request, method, Config, or Helpers changes visible on the PendingRequest side. Do not copy the body-processing steps from the other side into this tree just because both issues appear in request-stack consolidation.

## Gaps That Remain

`SAL-213` is the maintenance entry point for this anomaly boundary; the card record has confirmed the scope, but one point remains unconfirmed. The link is used only to find that maintenance record. It is still not possible to confirm the actual path where traversal or request progression stops; after obtaining the directory provided by the caller, reproduce the issue along the actual path and add back both the stopping location and the object before entry. Until these two items are available, PendingRequest can serve only as a code entry point and cannot be written as the anomaly origin point.

versions.body:
# OAuth Scope Decision Record

This record was left earlier than the related card. Initially, someone noticed calls without scope in the authorization code flow, but the issue did not manifest as a directly identifiable anomaly: the request still continued, and the difference lay in what the authorization parameters ultimately looked like. The old entry therefore continued to point to `src/Traits/OAuth2/AuthorizationCodeGrant.php`, and later investigations often started here as well.

The initial draft contained a judgment that was not sufficiently precise: since scope might have no value, leave `scope=` on authorization URL, so that the request string would look more uniform. At the time, "not provided" was understood as "the value is empty." This wording is retained below because someone in the old branch did investigate the issue on that basis; it is not the approach that should be continued now.

> Old judgment: when scope is missing, output `scope=`, which can reduce the need to distinguish between parameter shapes later.

This judgment did not resolve the caller's semantics. Not passing scope means that the caller made no scope selection; adding the scope key with an empty value, however, has already constructed an explicit parameter. Both may be accepted by some authorization servers, or they may be handled differently at a later parameter layer, but SDK should not change the former into the latter merely to make the string form consistent.

## The three approaches considered at the time

The first was to add an empty key. It was the easiest to implement: whenever the input was missing, write `scope=` into the URL parameter. The main reason supporting this approach was that the URL shape would remain stable, so debugging would not produce samples that sometimes had the key and sometimes did not. That is also where the problem lies. What remains stable is the output text, not the caller's original input; once downstream logic makes decisions based on whether the key exists, this rewrite is no longer harmless formatting cleanup.

The second was to add a default scope. Someone proposed putting a commonly used scope into the Authorization Code Grant so that every caller would not have to handle the same thing. This approach was not adopted. The default scope belongs to a server-side convention, Connector configuration, or the choice of a specific integration; it is not something the trait can decide arbitrarily. Putting it here would also cause a call that deliberately omitted scope to receive an authorization scope it did not choose.

The third was to preserve the omission. This is not a simplification rule saying that "all empty inputs are the same," nor does it promise that any OAuth server should accept requests without scope. It only limits the action at this layer: when the caller does not provide scope, the grant trait does not add a scope parameter, fill in a default value, or manufacture an explicit empty key. Values already provided by the caller continue to be handled by the subsequent request-construction layer.

This time, the third approach was retained. The decision is deliberately narrow: Authorization Code Grant must not normalize omission on its own. The available material is insufficient to establish here a uniform rule for whether an explicitly supplied empty string should be retained, rejected, or interpreted by a later parameter layer. Putting that case into the trait as well would only expand an unconfirmed interface constraint to all callers.

## Why the old entry is still worth keeping

The references visible in the file header are `DateTimeImmutable`, `Saloon\Helpers\Date`, `InvalidArgumentException`, and `Saloon\Contracts\Request`. This adjacency is enough to indicate the direction for investigation: Authorization Code Grant is not merely a URL string-concatenation point; it also touches the authorization flow's date state, input validation, and Request. Early on, scope omission was directly classified as "empty-value repair" within the trait, overlooking the fact that the parameters would also be passed to the request object layer.

However, these references do not constitute evidence for scope encoding. `DateTimeImmutable` and `Date` cannot establish how a missing parameter should be output; `InvalidArgumentException` only indicates adjacency with input validation; and `Request` suggests continuing to follow the parameter handoff. The old record once described these objects as supporting evidence that "the grant layer is responsible for OAuth configuration." That summary was too broad and is now marked as no longer applicable.

> Deprecated summary: since the trait touches dates, validation, and Request at the same time, it should organize the authorization parameters uniformly here.

The actual decision did not add a scope-normalization function next to the trait. Such an entry point would try to consume omission, empty strings, and other forms that might appear later, without any basis for saying that it has the authority to interpret these inputs. The farther parameter semantics are from the call site, the harder it becomes during later investigation to see who actually chose the scope.

## Branches during the investigation

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Scope not provided
    Scope not provided --> Preserve omission: Do not add a default value
    Scope not provided --> Do not use an empty key: Do not write scope=
    Scope not provided --> Do not use a default scope
    Explicit empty value --> TBD
```

"TBD" in the diagram does not treat an explicit empty value as an error; it preserves the question that the initial draft did not answer. When investigating a specific integration, first check whether the caller passed scope; if not, confirm that the grant layer did not add a value, then follow the Request parameter handoff and inspect the URL assembly. If the caller passed an empty value, do not use the conclusion about omission to decide the matter on its behalf.

This sequence also explains why no fixed authorization URL parameter order was required here. Whether parameter order has compatibility significance is something the specific assembly point and existing examples should answer. The current material only confirms that the user path permits OAuth scope omission; it does not provide an ordering rule that covers every Connector or authorization server. Changing the order to handle omission would instead tie two independent issues together.

## Changes after the related card

This user path was later assigned to SAL-216. The card still describes using existing tests or examples to trigger OAuth scope omission and writing the user paths that are not yet covered back into the card. It provides a tracking entry point, not a complete specification for authorization parameters; what is preserved here is the decision about why scope was not added inside the trait at the time.

The card later returned to the actual maintenance entry point and then moved into the in-progress state. This change shows that the issue did not disappear automatically just because the decision was recorded: existing tests or examples are still needed to bring the omitted-parameter path to the surface. It also did not change this page's boundaries. If an integration requires scope, that integration should provide the parameter explicitly rather than putting the default scope back into Authorization Code Grant.

## A few words for those reading the old branch later

- Omission and an explicit empty value are treated separately; the former is not rewritten inside the grant trait.
- `scope=` was an approach considered but not adopted in the initial draft; "more stable" in the old text referred only to the string shape.
- Do not add a project-wide default scope. The existing material does not provide that default value, nor does it delegate scope selection to the trait.
- Whether the authorization server accepts an omitted scope, how it handles an empty value, and whether parameter order is significant still need to be confirmed in the specific request construction and examples.

This page is still referenced mainly because it preserves a reason for rejection: do not use local default behavior to override an omission deliberately left by the caller. The early idea about an empty key is outdated, but retaining it makes clear to people who later read the old changes that what was avoided at the time was not an ordinary string-concatenation problem.

versions.body:
# Caller Dual-State Incident Postmortem

The initial account was brief: an integration tester opened a client entry point and saw current content that differed from the old record. The old record said PSR-7, while the entry point provided another current revision. Screenshots and old links were available, but the account, workspace, entry-point read time, and complete call sample had not been collected in one place. As a result, "the same object has two states" quickly became the on-site description, before the object relationship had been checked.

At the time, I treated the two different current revisions as coexisting results for the same object. This judgment did not come from the client's object identifier or a complete request; the entry points with the same name simply looked identical. Looking back, what most needs to be preserved is not whether that judgment sounded convincing, but that it actually affected the actions taken: the original record was saved, further retries were stopped, and the recovery page did not overwrite the earliest divergence.

## Evidence Preserved in the First Version

The first version recorded only a few gaps:

- When first seen, PSR-7 differed from the old record.
- Preserve the material from the original entry point first, and stop further retries for now.
- Later, one request lifecycle could recover.
- Why Sender changed was still unknown.

"The same client entry point has two current states. PSR-7 differs from the old record; for now, handle this as the caller still retaining two sets of states. The request lifecycle has recovered; the change in Sender is still unknown." This was the working position at the time, not a completed reproduction report. It combined observation, handling, and speculation, making it easy for readers to interpret "the same entry point" as "the same object".

The first version also lacked a complete set of read conditions. It did not record whether the two reads used the same account, whether they were in the same workspace, or place the old record and recovery page in a single chronological sequence. It could only support "the content seen at two points in time differed", not "both sets of content must have come from the same object".

Stopping further retries did not fix the entry point either. This action only prevented new reads from changing the divergence initially observed. If only the last screenshot were kept after each retry, the later green page would cover up the earliest difference, leaving the person taking over unable to determine when the difference appeared. The original record, recovery page, and integration feedback were therefore retained separately.

The judgment in the first version was not marked as a hypothesis. In hindsight, it was reached too quickly, but the first version cannot be rewritten as though account or workspace differences had already been ruled out at the time. That version did not contain this material; the gap itself was part of the incident evidence.

## The Timeline Reconstructed Later

| Point in time | Evidence preserved | Action taken at the time |
|---|---|---|
| First divergence | The current entry point did not match the PSR-7 description in the old record | Save the original record and stop further retries |
| Recovery page appeared | At least one request lifecycle could continue | Save the recovery page separately |
| Conditions reexamined | A regular account and an administrator might represent different read conditions | Record the current revision separately |
| Read-only account awaiting approval | Could not immediately reread under the same conditions | Keep the blocker recorded; do not substitute the recovery page for reproduction |
| Old exit action cleanup | The pre-change routing snapshot still existed | Clean up the old action and retain the snapshot |
| Account or workspace switched | Stopped upon reaching the exit entry point | List the account, workspace, and entry point as observation conditions again |

This timeline was gradually reconstructed after the first version. At the time, the first version only knew that "the content differed" and "the path later recovered"; it did not know the specific results of verification with a regular account, or that read-only account approval would block rechecking. The later card actions therefore cannot be retroactively treated as verification already completed in the first version.

## Several Divergences in the Supplementary Notes

SALA-004 later listed post-recovery verification with a regular account separately: read the recovered adj-traits using a regular account, and record it separately from the current revision seen by the administrator. This action changed how the read conditions were documented, but did not preserve complete paired results for the two account types. It does not directly establish that the regular account and administrator necessarily saw different revisions, nor prove that either one was the original old entry point.

SALA-015 recorded the handoff scope. The read-only account needed for reproduction was still awaiting approval, and the item was temporarily stuck at a point where it could not be reviewed again immediately. This blocker explains why the recovery page was not immediately compared with the initial record under the same conditions, but a blocker is not a reproduction result. Content that was never read cannot be filled in with "it recovered later".

SALA-011 dealt with routing remnants for the old exit action. The pre-change routing snapshot was retained, and the action pointing to the old exit action was later deleted. This item shows that there really was an old entry point that needed cleanup; the card did not connect it to the two current revisions, nor provide a result showing its impact on a particular client read. It cannot, on its own, be the cause of the dual states.

SALA-018 required preserving the two states of traits-client-integration in the order they occurred, and first confirming whether they belonged to the same object. On 2026 year 1 month 6 day, the integration-testing case was handed over to a new person. The only public comment was: "Switched to another account or workspace, and stopped upon reaching the exit entry point." This sentence did not identify the specific entry point or provide the before-and-after outputs for the two states, but it brought the account and workspace back into the scope of observation.

These card actions made the conditions somewhat clearer than in the first version, but still did not provide a final explanation. An account change might alter the read conditions, and a workspace change might also alter the entry point seen; the old exit action was a separate cleanup target. They can appear together on the timeline and should not be compressed into an already-proven causal chain.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller client
    participant I as Current entry point
    participant R as Original record
    participant H as Recovery page
    participant K as Follow-up checks
    C->>I: Read current revision
    I-->>R: Does not match the old record
    R-->>C: Stop further retries
    C->>H: request lifecycle recovers
    K->>I: Read separately by account or workspace
    K-->>R: Object ownership of the two states still unconfirmed
```

The arrows in the diagram indicate only the order in which material was preserved. The mismatch between the current entry point and the old record was the earliest observation; stopping retries was a preservation action; the recovery page appeared later. Follow-up checks listed the account, workspace, and exit entry point again, but did not prove that these conditions could be fully aligned with the initial read.

## What the Misattribution Left Behind

### Entry Points with the Same Name Are Not Necessarily the Same Object

The first version treated identical entry-point names as approximate evidence of object identity. The name made "the same object has two sets of states" sound natural, but without an object identifier, a call sample, or reads under the same conditions, all that can be said is that the entry-point content differed at two points in time. "The same object" in the old title preserves the judgment made at the time; it cannot be treated as the result of a completed check.

This is also why the initial PSR-7 difference cannot directly implicate Sender. The material contains no before-and-after states for Sender, no record of its involvement in the two reads, and no indication that its change occurred at the same time as the request lifecycle recovery. Sender was an unexplained term in the first version; the second version can flag this gap, but cannot choose a cause for it.

### Recovery Is Not an Explanation

The request lifecycle could continue later, indicating that at least one caller path had moved past the initial stall. It did not indicate that the other entry point had disappeared, or that the content in both places had ever belonged to the same call. The recovery page preserves the path that could be used later, not a root-cause explanation for the dual states.

If only the post-recovery green result were retained, the person taking over would not see why retries were stopped initially. The recovery page and original record need to be viewed side by side: the former shows that a path became available later, while the latter preserves the earliest difference. Neither can overwrite the other.

The current revisions for the regular account and administrator also cannot be merged without outputs. SALA-004 only separated the verification conditions, and SALA-015 also shows that read-only account approval once blocked reproduction. There is no complete comparison between the regular account and administrator here, so "recorded separately" cannot be rewritten as "the pages have been confirmed to differ".

### The Old Exit Action Is Not a Ready-Made Root Cause

The routing remnants for the old exit action have a separate cleanup record, and the pre-change snapshot was also retained. Because the cleanup time was close to the recovery record, it was easy at the time to interpret it as the step that caused the dual states. But the card did not show which client the old route affected, or which current revision it changed.

A more defensible ordering is: the old exit action needed cleanup; the account or workspace might alter the read conditions; whether the two states belonged to the same object had still not been checked completely. Cleanup results cannot substitute for object ownership, and account changes cannot substitute for before-and-after routing outputs.

### One Comment Cannot Expand the Scope of Reproduction

"Switched to another account or workspace, and stopped upon reaching the exit entry point" is an incomplete observation. It did not specify the entry point where things stopped, provide outputs from before and after the switch, or state that the exit entry point was the same as the initial client entry point. It cannot be expanded into "the account has explained the dual states".

However, this comment exposed the actual gap in the first version: the observer might have read entry points with the same name under different accounts or workspaces. Because the first version did not record these conditions, the two points in time appeared to show two stable states of the same object. The comment should be preserved, but cannot be filled out into a complete incident reproduction.

## Impact and Recovery

The most direct impact was that the entry-point descriptions in the integration-testing material could not directly substitute for one another. When a caller used a particular current revision to determine adaptation boundaries, they might receive a different context than at another point in time. Real call samples and integration feedback involving the client cannot be reduced to just the recovery page, or later readers will mistakenly believe that the adaptation work was always based on the same entry-point content.

The impact window can be counted from the first discovery that the old record did not match the current entry point until at least one request lifecycle recovered. The material does not provide failure results for all callers or the availability of both entry points at every point in time, so these are not the start and end times of a complete service outage. What can be confirmed here is that the records diverged, and a path was available to continue later.

After recovery, the original record still had value. It preserved the content from when the divergence first appeared, the recovery page preserved the path that could continue later, and the handoff record preserved why a reread under the same conditions was not performed immediately. Deleting any one of these materials would make another carry a meaning it had never carried before.

Actions already taken include: saving the earliest original record; stopping further retries; preserving the recovery page separately; distinguishing the conditions under which regular accounts and administrators read the current revision; retaining the routing snapshot from before the old exit action was changed; and recording the two traits-client-integration states in the order they occurred. These actions each preserve incident evidence; together, they do not constitute a root-cause conclusion.

What remains incomplete is reproduction under the same conditions. The scope of regular-account verification was raised, but the available material does not provide complete outputs paired with the administrator's results. The read-only account was awaiting approval, and a comment about switching accounts or workspaces appeared afterward; the entry point, time, and call sample were not completed together. The recovery page therefore cannot fill in the missing read results.

The assessment of Sender is also incomplete. There are no before-and-after versions, call relationships, or read results that can prove it changed. The first version retained Sender because the explanation was still disconnected after recovery occurred; the second version only puts that gap back in its original place, without elevating a nearby term into a cause.

## Questions Still on the Page

- Whether the two different current revisions belong to the same client object.
- Whether the original record and recovery page were obtained using the same account and workspace.
- Whether the current revisions seen by the regular account and administrator actually differ.
- Whether the stop at the exit entry point occurred on the call path containing the two states.
- Whether the routing remnants for the old exit action affected any entry-point read.
- Whether Sender really changed before and after the request lifecycle recovered.

These questions cannot answer one another. Routing cleanup cannot replace an account comparison, account changes cannot replace object checks, and recovery results cannot replace before-and-after records for Sender. The available material only shows that these divergences were observed or handled at different times; it does not provide evidence that covers all of them.

## Appendix of the Old Example: The Handling Position at the Time

> The same client entry point has two current states. PSR-7 differs from the old record; for now, handle this as the caller still retaining two sets of states. The request lifecycle has recovered; the change in Sender is still unknown.

This old example is no longer suitable as an explanation of object relationships, but is still retained because it explains why the original material was saved first rather than continuing to refresh the entry point. It also preserves the unresolved Sender issue from the time. Replacing this passage with "the account conditions have not yet been confirmed" would lose the stronger judgment actually adopted in the first version.

Another position added later was: switched to another account or workspace, and stopped upon reaching the exit entry point. It adds one observation condition beyond the old example, but does not provide enough comparative outputs. Both passages remain here: the former represents the earliest working hypothesis, and the latter represents the reproduction gap discovered later; they cannot be joined into a complete conclusion.

SALA-004, SALA-011, SALA-015 and SALA-018 correspond respectively to regular-account verification, the old exit action, the handoff and read-only account blocker, and checking the sequence of the two states. They can serve as entry points for further review of the incident evidence. DOC-31 records an approach that was not adopted, and is not rewritten on this page as the cause of the incident.

This page currently closes on only three points: the earliest divergence was not overwritten by the recovery page; at least one caller path later recovered; and the cause of the apparent dual states, as well as its relationship to Sender, remains unconfirmed. The old title and the first version's judgment remain archived because they are part of how the incident was understood and where that understanding stalled.

This checklist originally defined "exit" very narrowly: find a keyword, see a request object once, and then start collecting the evidence. The actual window records left behind later did not support that judgment. The old section is still retained because it explains why some old windows contain only a partial result; it is no longer the operating sequence for the current entry point.

The checklist covers only actual call samples, adapter boundaries, and integration feedback for traits-client-integration. What needs to be confirmed is the exit action, the last visible result, and whether adj-traits ended its own temporary action. Release success is signed off separately by the corresponding owner; this checklist does not make that determination.

## Two Prompts on the Old Page

Early versions instructed us to look for `backoff` in `docs/adj-traits/release/traits-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md` and, after seeing `PendingRequest`, not to clean up the state; stop if `retry` does not appear. These sentences are retained for reviewing old windows, but they cannot be used to conclude that the current entry point is still valid.

Another old prompt treated the "expiration action" as a directly executable signal to close the window. Later page feedback explicitly stated that the action was no longer valid, and the entry-point prompt still had not been updated. When you encounter this prompt, do not continue following the old wording: pause closing the window, confirm the current materials entry point, and then decide whether the checks within this page's scope can still be performed. Until that is confirmed, do not interpret a blank record as completed.

## Exit Sequence for This Run

1. **First capture the last sample.**
   - [ ] Open the checklist file and retain the original input for this client call, the version at the time, and the first visible result.
   - [ ] If a rejection path exists, retain it alongside the success path; do not retain only the success result from a later rerun.
   - [ ] If a diagnostic action changed the state, label that output separately; do not use it to overwrite the initial result.

2. **Check intermediate records.**
   - [ ] Check whether the artifact or status for `PendingRequest` can be found within the window.
   - [ ] "Success" in the logs cannot substitute for the artifact or status. It only indicates that success was recorded somewhere; it does not indicate that this window meets the exit conditions.
   - [ ] If an intermediate record is missing, leave it blank according to the convention in SALA-005. Do not fill this blank with a neighboring call, an old screenshot, or a similarly named output.

3. **Remove temporary actions.**
   - [ ] Remove the temporary permissions and bypasses provisioned for this integration test.
   - [ ] Then check whether the window is still receiving new work; if new samples are still coming in, stop the exit process and keep the window in an observable state first.
   - [ ] Keep the last visible result in the same window record both before and after cleanup, so you do not end up with only "cleaned up" and lose the object that was present at the time.

4. **Recovery is not overwriting.**
   The old record for SALA-001 contains only the rollback_checked marker. It shows that rollback was checked at the time, but does not show that the post-recovery result matches the original state. When recovery is needed, first append the recovery result alongside the original failed window; retain the original failed window, original object, and original result. If the recovery action itself changes the input or sample, start a separate record; do not edit the old result.

5. **Hand off outstanding items.**
   SALA-008 already has handoff confirmation. Before closing the window, still record which exit action remains, which result was not observed, and the handoff entry point. Writing only "the project team will continue to monitor" is not enough; if there is no clear handoff entry point, keep the window open and do not complete the cleanup.

## Stop Conditions

If any of the following occurs, stop at the current window and do not expand the scope of the check:

- The checklist page provides only an invalid expiration prompt, and no current entry point that can be verified can be found;
- A success path exists, but the rejection path or intermediate record was not retained;
- `PendingRequest` appears only in the log text, with no corresponding artifact or status;
- The temporary bypass is ready to be removed, but new client-call samples are still arriving;
- The post-recovery result can only overwrite the old record and cannot be retained alongside it.

After stopping, retain the original input and last visible result already collected. Do not invent entries to fill blanks just to make the checklist look complete, and do not bring adapter decisions made outside the window into it.

## Older Records Still Applicable

SALA-012 requires appending the recovery result to the "traits-client-integration Exit Window Checklist" and not overwriting the original failed window; this still applies. The rollback marker and invalid-entry prompt in SALA-001 are useful only as historical clues. The checklist file remains a reference point, but its old page header cannot replace the current release or handoff decision.

DOC-31 records an integration path that was not adopted. Do not restate that path here; review the original record only if the exit action actually reaches that branch.

# Alternatives for Caller Integration Testing

`traits-client-integration` leaves a narrow choice this time: keep caller integration testing under `compatibility`, or split `Connector` out separately. Neither route has yet become an integration rule. What the existing records do confirm is that the two failure exits in the related materials are different; this is enough to cast doubt on continuing to treat them as the same kind of compatibility issue, but not enough to assign a caller to each exit or finalize the migration sequence.

The initial preference was to retain `compatibility`, for a straightforward reason: the legacy entry point is already close to the callers, and leaving the name unchanged for now seemed likely to require fewer changes. The problem with this approach is not the legacy entry point itself, but that it would continue to lump different adaptation failures together. When a failure appears during integration testing, readers can only start by guessing whether it comes from the legacy compatibility branch or from a caller that has not yet been connected; these two cases require different handling.

`Connector` is the candidate object proposed to make this distinction. After the split, the caller integration boundary can be recorded separately, while compatibility behavior at the legacy entry point remains in place for checking. The proposal does not assume that splitting out an object will automatically eliminate compatibility logic, nor does it treat the object's name as evidence that migration is already complete. It only attempts to first separate "why the caller enters here" from "why the legacy path still exists".

## Two Routes

**Continue along `compatibility`.**

This route is suitable when it has been confirmed that most callers are indeed just reusing the same legacy behavior. Its weakness is that there is still no place to account for the observation that the failure exits differ: whenever another call sample is added, it will first be necessary to determine whether the sample is validating the compatibility branch or exposing the integration boundary. If this route is retained, it should at least be possible to explain why the different exits still belong to the same compatibility surface; those materials are currently missing.

**Split out `Connector` first.**

This route does not require moving all callers immediately. It first places an existing call sample alongside a separate integration boundary and retains the legacy entry point, so that the failure exits encountered on both sides can be compared. The benefit is that it exposes the unknowns rather than hiding them under a compatibility name. The cost is equally clear: caller Fang Ke may still depend on behavior at the legacy entry point, and once the split goes beyond what has been confirmed, it will bring gaps in the migration directly into integration testing.

The current recommendation is to keep `Connector` as the priority route for a trial, without removing `compatibility` as the alternative in the opposite direction. Here, "priority" only means arranging the comparison first, not that the latter has already been judged wrong.

## What the Trial Should Record

The trial starts with an existing call sample. The sample should record its input, the result obtained, and the object name that could be identified at the time; without these, neither a single success nor a single failure is enough to show whether the integration boundary is clear. Then add an input in the opposite direction. The review does not need to include all callers at once, only to confirm whether the two inputs enter along the same section of the call path and whether their failure exits can be recorded distinctly.

The input in the opposite direction is a clear gap at present, with no concrete construction provided and no results to draw on. It cannot be replaced with "no errors so far", much less can `Connector` be assumed suitable for the remaining callers just because the first sample works. If the second input still cannot be matched to a particular caller or a particular type of failure exit, the record should leave it unverified rather than supply a seemingly reasonable attribution.

`middleware` is another point that cannot be skipped. Its current callers have not yet been confirmed, so it cannot be assumed to migrate naturally along with `Connector`, nor can it be folded into the legacy compatibility branch based on its name alone. If the trial reveals that `middleware` still depends on an unconfirmed legacy entry point, preserve that dependency first, then decide whether to expand the sample set further; do not assign users to it just to make the split look tidy.

## Migration Boundaries

This is not a proposal to replace the legacy entry point. The existing materials contain no start date, no list of callers that have completed migration, and no indication of who is actually carrying out the migration, so no rollout batches are set here. The trial of `Connector` only adds a boundary that can be checked, without changing the fact that the legacy entry point can still be inspected.

For the legacy entry point migration index, see DOC-32; the paths listed there are not repeated here. For this proposal, the questions that must be answered before migration are: whether a call sample depends on behavior available only at the legacy entry point, and whether the split-out boundary can place the previously conflated failure exits in separate, readable locations. If the first question is unanswered, even a small migration should not be treated as low-risk; if the second question is unanswered, adding an object is not sufficiently justified either.

One easily confused situation needs to be called out separately: incomplete samples do not mean the route has failed. If only the opposite-direction input is missing, add the sample and leave the route undecided; if both inputs show that the failure exits still cannot be distinguished after the split, compare `compatibility` and `Connector` again rather than treating the former as the default fallback. Keeping the comparison open this way avoids writing "the materials are incomplete" and "the proposal offers no benefit" as the same conclusion.

## Rollback Point

The rollback point is set before migrating additional callers. Stop expanding the scope of the split if any of the following occurs: the input in the opposite direction has left no comparable record; `middleware` still depends on an unconfirmed legacy entry point; the exits after the split still cannot be distinguished from the caller integration boundary. Stopping expansion does not mean deleting objects already retained or erasing the comparison process, and the legacy entry point should remain available for checking.

The current materials do not establish whether rollback should consist only of restoring the legacy entry point. If the migration cost later turns out to outweigh the benefit of the distinctions gained through the split, `compatibility` can be revisited for reassessment; that assessment must still retain the different failure exits already observed, rather than judging solely by the amount of change. Conversely, if only one call sample is missing, add that sample first rather than turning a local gap into a reason to roll back the entire route.

Still unresolved are the actual callers of `middleware`, the form of the opposite-direction input, and whether rollback involves only the legacy entry point. Until actual records answer these questions, `Connector` is only a candidate boundary for comparison; the route along `compatibility` also remains on the table. The related draft is located at `docs/adj-traits/proposals/not-adopted-Traits-client-integration-approach.md`.

# Caller Entry Point Migration Notes

For the samples seen during caller integration testing, don't judge whether migration is complete solely by the new names in the directory. This page tracks the entry points still used by clients: the old entry point is the call on the `request lifecycle` side, and the proposed destination is the separate `Sender`. The two have different failure exits, so a replacement cannot be treated as just a rename.

The index file is at `docs/adj-traits/migration/current-entry-old-entry-migration-index.md`. When handling each caller, first fill in its name in that file, then confirm whether it actually enters through the old entry point or `Sender`; leave entries without actual samples blank, and don't infer them from similar clients.

|Index status|Action|
|---|---|
|Still enters through `request lifecycle`|Keep the old call, record the failure exit reproduced by this callFang Ke, then prepare an integration change that only switches the entry point.|
|Already enters through `Sender`|Check whether the failure exit still matches the old path; if not, do not expand the migration batch any further.|
|Entry point unknown|Do not move code; only record the missing call samples in the index.|
|Old and new coexist|First determine which entry point the caller actually sends through, then handle the legacy call at the other location.|

Sequence the migration by caller, not by traits directory. Start with a client whose actual sending behavior is already visible, keep the original entry point available, then switch that client to `Sender`. After the change, check only the adaptation boundary and integration feedback at this location: if the send reaches a different failure exit, revert this caller's entry-point change and keep the old path. Don't delete the old calls as well just because another caller already has `Sender`.

The callers currently using `Response` have not yet been identified. Do not use this item as a migration-complete signal or as the basis for deciding whether to delete the old entry point. If you encounter clients in the index that only return or only consume `Response`, mark them as pending verification first; without call samples, do not include them in the `Sender` batch.

When restoring the old path, first revert that caller's integration change for `Sender`, then confirm that it still enters through the original `request lifecycle`. Restoration applies only to callers that have already been migrated; do not clean up old entry points that have not yet been migrated. If the failure exit still differs from what it was before migration after rollback, stop further migration and leave that client's samples, entry-point assessment, and differences alongside the index file.

Confirm whether migration is complete against actual consumers: it should be possible to identify the entry point currently used by every migrated client in the index, and every retained call in the old entry point should map to a caller that still uses it. A new entry point appearing in the directory, or the traits themselves being loadable, does not mean callers have switched. Leave old entries that cannot be traced back marked as stale, and wait for new integration feedback before filling them in.

# Release Automation Exit Window Procedure

This checklist retains the closure criteria from an old window. It covers only the exit actions, the last visible result, and the exit action for adj-contracts; whether the release succeeded must be signed off separately by the corresponding owner. The entry point is `docs/adj-contracts/release/contracts-release-automation-exit-window-checklist.md`; the body and attachments are maintained by Contracts · Release Automation.

## Gates from the Old Window

The initial version treated `multipart` as a reminder to preserve the state and treated whether `PSR-7` appeared as a gate for continuing the closeout. The initial version had no recovery result for the shared environment and did not explain how to return to the original state after a failure, so this judgment remains. It shows which step the process had stopped at then; it cannot by itself prove that the release passed.

"Stop if `PSR-7` is missing" remains as recorded in the old record. If the window retains only success text in the logs, do not use those words in place of the last actually retained result; first record where the original result is located, then take any further action. A recovery result added to the page later cannot be backfilled to show that the initial version had already been completed.

## Before Closing the Window

- [ ] Record the checklist path, the location of the last result, and whether the current entry point can still be opened.
- [ ] Verify whether the queue is still accepting new work. If it is, stop closing the window; do not remove the bypass while allowing new work into the same window.
- [ ] First verify whether collection and execution are enabled. If neither the current entry point nor the original current revision has corresponding evidence, leave the status unknown; do not fill it in as a zero result. SALC-004 is a lead for locating inconsistent collection status; it does not fill in the missing record for this checklist.
- [ ] Retain the first visible result, input, and version; a cleaned-up green record must not overwrite the original failed window.

## Verification After Recovery

1. Use a regular account to read the recovered adj-contracts, and record the result separately from the current revision visible to the administrator. If the regular account cannot read it, do not substitute the administrator's view. SALC-002 corresponds to this step; it checks the read after recovery, not sign-off for the entire release.
2. If the recovery action changed the original artifact, temporary configuration, or queue state, first append the location where the change occurred to the original window record, then stop comparing. The SALC-010 requirement is to append the recovery result to the "contracts-release-automation Exit Window Checklist," not rewrite the earlier failure record.
3. Record the last visible result before withdrawal. If the result was not retained, only a new summary string exists, or a new record has overwritten the old object, return to the stop point; do not check the checklist off as complete.

## Withdrawal Sequence

- [ ] Remove the accounts, workers, environments, or proxies borrowed for the window, and state the latest time for their return.
- [ ] Temporary access has been revoked, or there is a clearly identified handoff giver, receiver, and confirmation time. If any one is missing, do not announce the window exit; SALC-013 can be used to fill in the confirmation time for the on-call handoff.
- [ ] Confirm again that the queue is not still accepting new work. If new work enters after the bypass is removed, stop cleanup; do not merge the new and old results.
- [ ] Leave unfinished exit actions in the window record and hand them to the corresponding owner to decide whether to open another window.

## Stop and Rollback

If any of the following occurs, stop at the current action: the current entry point and the original current revision both lack collection or execution status; the regular-account result cannot be documented alongside the administrator result; the queue is still accepting new work; temporary access has not been revoked and no handoff record exists; or a new recovery record is prepared to replace the old failed window.

If withdrawal has already started but the queue is found not to have stopped, restore the queue's intake state to its pre-withdrawal state, retain this run's last result, and then leave the decision to the corresponding owner. If the recovery process has already changed the state, mark subsequent results as changed and no longer compare them directly with the original failed window. Do not write "can read after recovery" as "release succeeded" here.

## Handoff

Write the handoff record with the handoff giver, receiver, confirmation time, location of the last result, and any unfinished withdrawal actions. SALC-007 are used to review zero-result collection status; SALC-013 are used to fill in handoff information. Other release decisions remain with the original owner for confirmation.
